CLASS 23 · THE MUSIC ROOM

Welcome to the Music Room.

The third room of the school, beside the Library and the School Garden: instruments on the shelves, the words music uses on the wall, and the people — solo, duet, band, chorus, conductor, singer, orchestra — who fill the room with sound. Every tile below opens its own flashcard page, and every card page has a download button and one game to play tonight.

THE INSTRUMENT SHELF

Thirty-three instruments, from accordion to xylophone.

Everything on the room’s shelves, one card each: strings you bow, keys you press, drums you boom and the small ones you shake, click and squeeze. Tap any instrument to open its own step-by-step lesson — what it is, how it makes its sound and how to build a home version tonight.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Accordion — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the accordion’s one big secret: nothing is plucked or hit — the player BREATHES the instrument, squeezing air through little metal tongues called reeds.

What is this?

An accordion is a squeeze-box: two wooden ends joined by folding bellows, with keys and buttons on the ends. Push and pull the bellows while pressing keys, and air rushes past reeds — the reeds hum, and that is the music.

What does it mean?

Every other instrument on the shelf waits for the player’s hands alone. The accordion waits for AIR — and the hands’ job is to be the lungs. Squeeze slowly for long sleepy sounds, fast for short jumpy ones: the same notes, two entirely different moods.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three accordion ideas: the bellows are the lungs — no squeeze, no sound, ever; inside are reeds, tiny metal tongues that hum when air brushes them; and push-pull makes the shape of the song — long squeezes for slow, quick pumps for jumpy.

Why this matters

The accordion teaches air flow better than any instrument a child can hold: you can SEE the lung. Once squeezing makes sound make sense, the flute, trumpet and every breath instrument arrive pre-understood.

What it teaches

Cause-and-effect with continuous control (squeeze strength = volume and length), push-pull bilateral rhythm, and the breath connection — the first instrument on the shelf that breathes.

Words to learn

accordionbellowssqueezereedpushpullair

Say this to your child

“"The accordion is a squeeze-box! See the folded middle — the bellows? That is its lung. Squeeze it shut and the air runs through little metal tongues called reeds — and the reeds SING. Squeeze slowly for a long, sleepy note… pump quickly for a short, jumpy one. Your hands are the breath!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is an accordion — the instrument you breathe by squeezing."
  2. Paper bellows: fold a paper fan, squeeze it shut slowly, open it slowly — that closing and opening IS the bellows.
  3. The reed idea: hum with the back of the hand on the throat — feel the buzz. Tiny metal reeds buzz the same way when air brushes them.
  4. The squeeze game: long slow squeeze = sleepy sound; quick pump-pump = jumpy sound. Same hands, different songs.
  5. Play the push-pull game below and close: "squeeze to sing."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Accordion" sits in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly accordion illustration below — the folded bellows exactly as the squeeze-box looks.

Ask your child

"What does the accordion use to make air move?" "What are the little metal tongues called?" "What happens if we stop squeezing?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The bellows are its lungs!" "Squeeze — and the reeds sing!" or the game report: "Slow squeeze is sleepy, pump-pump is jumpy!"

Out in the real world

Accordions live at folk festivals, polka bands and grandma’s cupboard — and their bellows live in every paper fan and camera pump. Fold a fan, pump a foot pump: squeeze-sound is everywhere once you hear it.

Try it together

Push-Pull Duet: one player folds a paper fan "bellows" and pumps slow-slow; the other hums a note only WHILE the fan closes. Squeeze = singing, open = silence. Swap. Then the mood game: "sing me a sleepy squeeze… now a jumpy one!" The hands learn what the lungs do — that is the whole accordion, played on paper.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the folded middle called? What hums inside? What happens when we stop squeezing?" The bellows, the reeds, silence — three answers and the squeeze-box has sung.

Parent tips

If no accordion is near, the paper fan IS the lesson — the push-pull control transfers perfectly. And name the reed buzzing on the throat first: feeling the buzz turns "reeds" from a word into a sensation.

This lesson pairs with the Accordion flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

Bagpipes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bagpipes’ clever trick: fill a bag with air first, then squeeze the bag steadily — which is why the sound never has to stop for a breath.

What is this?

Bagpipes are a wind instrument with a bag: the player blows air into the bag through a pipe, tucks the bag under the arm, and squeezes it to push air through the melody pipe and the long drone pipes that hum one steady note.

What does it mean?

Most wind instruments breathe note-by-note. The bagpipe BANKS its breath: fill the reservoir, then squeeze it out evenly. That banking is why a piper can play without pausing — and why the sound rolls across a whole valley.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three bagpipe ideas: the bag is an air piggy-bank — blow it full first, squeeze it second; the long pipes are drones — they hum ONE deep steady note the whole time, like a musical shadow; and the little melody pipe on top plays the tune over the drone.

Why this matters

The drone is the lesson’s gift: one note that never stops, under everything. Children who can hear the drone have learned harmony’s first secret — a sound can sit UNDER a sound.

What it teaches

Air storage thinking (fill-then-use), sustained-versus-moving sound layers, arm-squeeze pressure control, and the great fun of a sound you can argue about.

Words to learn

bagpipesbagdronesqueezeblowsteadypipes

Say this to your child

“"Bagpipes work in two steps! Step one: blow the bag FULL of air — a piggy-bank of breath. Step two: squeeze the bag with your arm, nice and steady, and the air sings through the pipes. The long pipes hum ONE deep note that never stops — the drone — and the little pipe on top plays the tune over it. Fill first, squeeze steady!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is bagpipes — a bag of air with pipes sticking out."
  2. The banking trick: blow up a paper bag, squeeze it slowly — the air comes out LONG after the breath ended. That is the piper’s secret pocket of air.
  3. The drone: hum one low note and HOLD it while a partner taps a rhythm — the held hum is the drone, the taps are the tune. Both at once = bagpipes.
  4. The squeeze: steady arm pressure keeps the sound even — squeeze-everything-out-fast and the song dies. Pipers are patient squeezers.
  5. Play the fill-and-squeeze game below and close: "fill first, squeeze steady."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Bagpipes" is printed in big navy capitals inside the frame, with a friendly bagpipe illustration below — the bag and its pipes exactly as the instrument looks.

Ask your child

"What does the player do first — squeeze or fill?" "What do the long pipes hum?" "Why does the sound never need to stop for breath?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The bag is an air piggy-bank!" "The drone hums under the tune!" or the classic: "It sounds like singing AND complaining!"

Out in the real world

Pipers lead parades in Scotland, New Zealand and Canada — listen for the drone across a park: one long note under everything, unmissable. And the air-bag trick lives in every air mattress and whoopee cushion: banking air is a household physics.

Try it together

Cushion Bagpipes: a cushion under the arm is the bag. Fill it: three big pretend breaths, patting it fatter. Then squeeze steadily while HUMMING one drone note — and a partner taps the melody on a pot lid. Swap: the hummer drones, the squeezer taps. The drone under the tune — Scotland’s great sound, built from a cushion.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is filled first? What hums one steady note? What plays the tune?" The bag, the drones, the melody pipe — three answers and the pipes are ready.

Parent tips

The drone game needs no instrument and no noise-tolerance: humming is free. And embrace the argument the card starts — lovely or loud, the piper does not care; the valley hears it either way.

This lesson pairs with the Bagpipes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Banjo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the banjo as a drum wearing strings: its round skin face is why every plink is brighter and bouncier than a guitar’s — plucking with a drum’s voice.

What is this?

A banjo is a string instrument with a round body: a drum-like face stretched over a hoop, a long neck with frets, and strings you pluck or strum. The tight face makes the sound ring out bright and fast.

What does it mean?

Plucking is the skill here — but the banjo adds a physics surprise: the same pluck sounds different on a drum face. Children learn that the BODY of an instrument is part of the sound, not just the strings.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three banjo ideas: the face is a drum — tight, round, bright; plucking is one string, one finger, one plink; strumming is all the strings, one sweep — plink versus swish.

Why this matters

The banjo’s build-it-yourself cousin (rubber bands on a box) is the most famous home instrument in the world for a reason: plucking a tightened band teaches pitch, tension and the twang in one afternoon.

What it teaches

Pincer-grip plucking (fine motor), one-versus-all-strings contrast, rhythm patterns, and the tension-pitch idea — tighter band, higher plink.

Words to learn

banjopluckstrumtwangstringsfacebright

Say this to your child

“"The banjo is a drum wearing strings! Its face is round and tight like a drum — that is why every plink is bright as a bell. Pluck ONE string with one finger: plink. Strum ALL the strings with one sweep: swish! And you can build one today — rubber bands on a box, pencil bridge, and you are in the band."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a banjo — a drum with strings on its face."
  2. Point out the round face: "like a drum, right? Tight and round. That is why the banjo BRIGHTLY twangs while a guitar hums deeper."
  3. Pluck versus strum: one finger, one string, plink — all the strings, one sweep, swish. Do both on the card picture.
  4. Build the box banjo: an empty tissue box or shoebox, three rubber bands around it — plink! Slide a pencil under the bands as a bridge: plinker and louder!
  5. Play the plink pattern game below and close: "one string plinks, all strings swish."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Banjo" stands in big navy capitals in the rounded frame, with a friendly banjo illustration below — the round body and long neck exactly as the instrument looks.

Ask your child

"What is the banjo’s body like — a drum or a box of tissue?" "What is one string called? All the strings together?" "What happens to the plink if the band is tighter?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It’s a drum with strings!" "Plink is one, swish is all!" or the builder’s pride: "My box banjo has a pencil bridge!"

Out in the real world

Banjos drive bluegrass, folk and old-time dance music across the US — and their box-banjo cousins live in every kitchen drawer: rubber bands on a tin. Strum one today; the twang teaches itself.

Try it together

Plink-Pattern Band: box banjo ready. Call patterns: "plink-plink-PLINK" (two soft, one loud), then "plink… plink… swish!" The player follows the calls; the listener dances. Swap caller and player. Every pattern lands because plucking is instant — the fastest sound-to-hand connection on the whole shelf.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the body like? One string or all strings — which is plink? What tightens to raise the plink?" A drum face, one string, the rubber band — three answers and the twang is yours.

Parent tips

Tighter rubber bands genuinely sound higher — let the child retune by ear and discover pitch-tension themselves. And a pencil bridge under the bands is the magic upgrade; do not skip it.

This lesson pairs with the Banjo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bass Drum — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bass drum’s deep truth: it is less a sound than a FEELING — one big boom that everyone’s chest can feel, holding the whole band together like a heartbeat in boots.

What is this?

A bass drum is the biggest drum in the room: a huge round drum struck with a big soft mallet, booming one deep note at a time. In bands and parades it is the metronome everyone marches to.

What does it mean?

Pitch lives low: the bigger the drum, the deeper the boom — and deep sounds travel through the floor, the chair and your ribs. The bass drum is the first instrument a child plays with their body as well as their ears.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three bass-drum ideas: big drum = deep boom (size is pitch); the bass drum does not rush — it lands ONE steady beat and everything else arranges itself around it; and the mallet is big and soft because the drum is a friend, not a foe.

Why this matters

Feeling sound in the chest is the earliest music sense babies have — the bass drum names it, honours it, and hands the child the band’s most powerful job: keeping everyone together.

What it teaches

Steady beat keeping (the skill under all rhythm), size-pitch understanding, sound-vibration sensing through touch, and big-movement striking with control.

Words to learn

bass drumboombeatmalletsteadydeepheartbeat

Say this to your child

“"The bass drum is the biggest drum — and the biggest drum makes the deepest boom! You hear it, and you FEEL it in your chest: BOOM… BOOM… like a giant’s heartbeat. And that boom is the boss of the band: when it lands steady, every foot in the parade lands with it. One boom, all together!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the bass drum — the biggest boom in the room."
  2. Size is pitch: tap a big pot, tap a tiny cup — big things boom, small things ting. The bass drum is the biggest, so its boom is the deepest.
  3. Feel the beat: put a hand gently on a speaker or tap the floor — feel the thud in your palm. Deep sound is touchable.
  4. The heartbeat: BOOM… BOOM… slow and steady, like the giant’s heart. Steady beats let everyone march together.
  5. Play the heartbeat game below and close: "one boom, all together."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Bass Drum" sit in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the big drum below — exactly as it looks on the parade field.

Ask your child

"Which drum booms deepest — the biggest or the smallest?" "Where else can you FEEL the boom?" "What is the bass drum’s job in the band?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Big drum, deep boom!" "I felt it in my chest!" or the drummer’s pride: "I keep everybody together!"

Out in the real world

Bass drums march in every parade, thump in every rock band’s kick pedal and roll under every concert — and their deep booms live at home: the big pot, the floor tom of a sofa cushion. Feel for them.

Try it together

Heartbeat Band: one player is the BASS — a floor cushion or big pot with a sock mallet, landing BOOM… BOOM… steady as sleep. Everyone else joins one by one: shaker eggs, claps, table taps — each one landing WITH the boom. The bass player is the boss; when the boom speeds up, everybody does. Keep it going for a whole song. One boom, all together — that is the parade.

Understanding check

Ask: "Big drum makes what kind of sound? What is the bass drum’s job? What do we feel in our chest?" Deep boom, keeping the beat, the thud — three answers and the band marches.

Parent tips

Steady beats slow: four-year-olds rush. Model boom-breathing — in and out with each boom — and the tempo falls into place. And the sock mallet is non-negotiable: pots survive, eardrums thank you.

This lesson pairs with the Bass Drum flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bells — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches bells as the pitch ladder: a row of shiny metal notes standing in order, so the child can SEE low-to-high while their ears climb it.

What is this?

Bells (orchestral or glockenspiel style) are a row of metal bars or bells, laid out low to high: strike each one with a mallet and it rings one clear note. Together they are a ladder of pitch you can walk up and down.

What does it mean?

The bells make pitch VISIBLE: the small bar on the right really is the high note, the big bar on the left really is the low one. Size-pitch, seen in a row, struck one by one — the scale stops being abstract forever.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three bells ideas: each bell is one note — one strike, one ding; the row is in ORDER — left is low, right is high; and the scale is the ladder — step up note by note, and the song "do-re-mi" is just the ladder climbed.

Why this matters

Pitch order is the doorway to every melody. The bells hand it over physically: step, step, step up the row — and every later instrument (piano keys, guitar frets) is just another ladder.

What it teaches

Size-pitch mapping, ordered sequencing (the scale is a sequence), mallet striking accuracy, and high-low listening discrimination.

Words to learn

bellspitchlowhighladderscaleding

Say this to your child

“"Bells are notes you can climb! Each bell rings one ding. And they stand in order like a ladder: the big bells on the left ring LOW, the small bells on the right ring HIGH. Ding your way up the row — step, step, step — and that climb is the scale, the staircase hiding inside every song."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "These are bells — a row of notes standing in order."
  2. The ladder law: point left — "small strike? no — big bell, LOW ding." Point right — "small bell, HIGH ding." Big-low, small-high: say it twice.
  3. Climb the ladder: ding each bell left to right, one step up each time — that climb is the scale, the staircase every song walks.
  4. Build the water bells: five glass jars, water at different levels — tap with a spoon. More water = lower ding. Line them up low to high, your own bell row.
  5. Play the stair game below and close: "big is low, small is high."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Bells" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the row of bells below — exactly as the pitch ladder looks.

Ask your child

"Which side rings low — the big bells or the small ones?" "What do we call the climb up the row?" "How many notes does one bell ring?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Big bell — low ding!" "I climbed the whole ladder!" or the jar builder’s pride: "More water sings lower!"

Out in the real world

Bells ring everywhere: doorbells, bicycle bells, school chimes, the ice-cream truck’s five-note call. And the water-jar set is a kitchen classic — five jars, one spoon, the whole scale on the table.

Try it together

Bell Stairs: lay five cards on the floor as bell-steps, low to high. Tap each "bell" (a jar, a pot, a clap-pitch) and step up as you ding — body and ears climb together. Then ring a melody: the ice-cream call, "hot cross buns" (three notes!), happy birthday’s first five steps. Every melody is the ladder climbed in a pattern.

Understanding check

Ask: "Big bell or small bell — which rings high? What is the row called? What is a melody made of?" Small, a ladder, the ladder climbed — three answers and the bells are ringing.

Parent tips

Let the child REORDER mixed-up jars by ear — fixing the ladder is better training than climbing a pre-fixed one. And whisper "do-re-mi" up the rungs: the syllables stick to the steps like glue.

This lesson pairs with the Bells flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Castanets — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the castanets — two little clappers that live on your fingers and click like talking beetles: the smallest instruments on the shelf with the quickest sound they make.

What is this?

Castanets are two shell-shaped pieces of wood joined by a cord: hold them in the palm and click the shells together with the fingers. Flamenco dancers wear them; whole orchestras borrow their chatter.

What does it mean?

Castanets train the fastest fine-motor music there is: the click is a finger squeeze, not an arm swing. Fast patterns — click-click-rest, clickety-click — live in fingers alone, which makes these two shells a fine-motor gym disguised as flamenco.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three castanet ideas: the click is a SQUEEZE — fingers press the shells together, not a bang; the cord loops over the finger so one hand holds both shells; and fast patterns are the game — click-click-rest is the first sentence the shells speak.

Why this matters

Of every instrument here, the castanets live closest to the hand: no stick, no mallet, no breath — just fingers. They grow the exact finger strength that pencils and scissors will ask for.

What it teaches

Finger isolation and squeeze control, fast alternating patterns, palm-steadiness while fingers work, and rhythm sentences — the click as a syllable.

Words to learn

castanetsclickshellsfingerssqueezepatternfast

Say this to your child

“"Castanets are two little shells that click in your palm! The secret is the SQUEEZE — fingers press the shells together, click! Not a bang, a click. Start talking: click-click-rest… click-click-rest… then the fast one: clickety-click! Your fingers are the fastest musicians in the whole Music Room."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "These are castanets — two little shells that click."
  2. The squeeze: clap your OWN fingers and thumb together — that snap is the castanet’s whole secret: a finger click, not a hand clap.
  3. Card castanets: two bottle caps glued (or taped) inside-card-out on folded card squares — hold both, click them together. Or two big buttons on fingers.
  4. The first sentence: click-click-REST. Say it, play it, three times. Then clickety-click (four fast) — the shells are talking!
  5. Play the click-pattern game below and close: "squeeze to speak."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Castanets" sits in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the pair below — the two shells and their cord exactly as they look.

Ask your child

"What makes the click — a bang or a finger squeeze?" "What holds the two shells together?" "What is the shells’ first sentence?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Click is a squeeze, not a bang!" "Clickety-click — the fast one!" or the flamenco shout: "Olé!"

Out in the real world

Castanets click in Spanish flamenco, in orchestras’ sneaky moments — and their cousins live on every kitchen bench: two spoons back-to-back, two bottle caps, a snap of fingers and thumb. Clicks are free.

Try it together

Click-Talk: the shells speak sentences and the other player copies — "click-click-rest", "clickety-click-click-rest", "click… clickety-click!" Then the flamenco finale: one player clicks a steady pattern, the other dances four big steps and shouts olé. Fingers fast, feet loud, pride enormous.

Understanding check

Ask: "What makes the sound? What is the first pattern? Where do flamenco dancers wear them?" The squeeze, click-click-rest, on their hands — three answers and the shells are talking.

Parent tips

If finger clicks frustrate, play on the knee first — knee-clicks build the pattern, palm-clicks arrive by themselves. And keep shells small and cord short: castanets are whisper-instruments with giant personalities.

This lesson pairs with the Castanets flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Cello — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the cello as the instrument you sit BEHIND and HUG — the only one on the shelf that rests against your body like a tall wooden friend, singing when the bow strokes it.

What is this?

A cello is the big low member of the violin family: you sit with it standing between your knees, its body resting against your chest, and draw a bow across the strings — or pluck them — to make deep, singing notes.

What does it mean?

Strings make sound two ways — pluck (short) and bow (long) — and the cello’s size makes the difference unmistakable: a plucked cello goes brrring, a bowed one goes oooooooh for as long as the arm lasts. The bow is a breath made of horsehair.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three cello ideas: you sit BEHIND it and it leans on you — the cello hug; the bow is horsehair drawn SLOWLY across the strings — slow bow, long song; and plucking (pizzicato!) is the string’s short way of talking.

Why this matters

The cello’s voice is the closest thing on the shelf to a human singing voice — deep enough to hum along with. Children who hum with a cello have found the instrument that most sounds like feelings.

What it teaches

Slow continuous bow control (a genuine fine-motor marvel), the two-voices contrast — pluck versus bow — posture with a big object, and low-pitch listening.

Words to learn

cellobowstringspluckpizzicatohugdeep

Say this to your child

“"The cello is the big singing string! You sit behind it and HUG it — it leans on your chest like a tall wooden friend. Pluck the string: brrring, short and spiky. Draw the bow slowly: oooooh — the string SINGS for as long as your arm keeps going slow. The bow is a breath made of horsehair."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a cello — the big string you sit behind and hug."
  2. The hug: sit on a chair, spread the knees, lean a cushion "cello" against the chest — that is the playing position, the cello hug.
  3. Two voices: pluck a rubber band on a box — brrring, short. Then "bow" it with a finger drawn slowly — ooooooh, long. Pluck is short, bow is long.
  4. The slow arm: real bows sing only when they travel SLOW and straight — glide a finger along the band at snail pace. Rush it and the sound stumbles.
  5. Play the long-song game below and close: "slow bow, long song."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Cello" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the cello and its bow below — exactly as the big string looks.

Ask your child

"Where does the cello sit when you play — on the floor or hugging you?" "Which is longer, pluck or bow?" "What is the bow made of?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I hug the cello!" "Pluck is short, bow is looong!" or the hum-along: "It sounds like a big person singing!"

Out in the real world

Cellos sit in every orchestra’s front row and hum under almost every movie’s saddest scene — and the hug position lives in every cushions-and-boxes cello a child builds. Hum with one on screen: the low friend sings back.

Try it together

Long-Song Contest: rubber-band box cello ready. One player plucks — count how short it was. Then bows (a slow finger) — how LONG can the oooh last? Beat yesterday’s record. Then the feelings game: "bow me a sleepy sound… a marching sound… a sad one." The same string says all three — the arm decides. That is the cello’s whole secret.

Understanding check

Ask: "How does the cello sit with you? What makes the long sound? What is plucking called?" The hug, the slow bow, pizzicato — three answers and the big string sings.

Parent tips

The slow arm is hard and wonderful — glide along the band at snail pace and count the seconds out loud. And honour pizzicato: naming the pluck with its Italian word makes children own it forever.

This lesson pairs with the Cello flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Clarinet — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the clarinet’s clever tongue: a thin sliver of cane called a reed sits against the player’s lip, and when breath rushes past — the reed quacks, honks and sings.

What is this?

A clarinet is a long black tube with silver keys and a mouthpiece holding one thin reed. Blow air past the reed and it vibrates — hundreds of times a second — and the tube turns the buzz into a warm, woody note.

What does it mean?

The reed is the lesson: a piece of wood that sings because air makes it flutter. Straw-demo it and the flutter is visible and audible in ten seconds — the clarinet’s whole magic, demystified at a kitchen table.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three clarinet ideas: the reed is a thin wooden tongue that flutters when you blow; the long black tube makes the flutter into a note — longer tube, lower honk; and the keys open and close holes to change the note as you play.

Why this matters

The straw-clarinet is the perfect first instrument build: cut the tip, blow, and it QUACKS. The child who hears their own straw reed has met the oboe, clarinet, saxophone and bassoon’s shared secret in one afternoon.

What it teaches

Breath control (long steady air), the vibration idea made audible, hole-covering sequencing, and straw-scissors fine motor for the build.

Words to learn

clarinetreedblowvibratekeystubehonk

Say this to your child

“"The clarinet has a secret tongue — a thin wooden sliver called a reed! When you blow, the reed flutters like a flag in the wind — flutter-flutter, hundreds of times a second — and the long black tube turns that buzz into a beautiful note. Want to meet a reed today? A drinking straw, cut to a point, will HONK for you."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a clarinet — a long black stick that sings with a wooden tongue."
  2. The reed: a thin sliver of cane on the mouthpiece. Blow past it — it flutters, or vibrates, faster than a hummingbird’s wing. That flutter IS the sound.
  3. Straw demo: flatten one end of a drinking straw, cut it to a point, blow — HONK! A straw reed, quacking. Trim the straw shorter: higher honk!
  4. The tube rule: longer tube, lower note — point at the long black tube on the card, then at the tiny piccolo card: opposites.
  5. Play the long-breath game below and close: "blow steady, reed sings."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Clarinet" leads in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the clarinet and its keys below — exactly as the black tube looks.

Ask your child

"What flutters inside the mouthpiece? What does the tube turn the flutter into? Which sings lower — a long tube or a short one?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The reed flutters like a flag!" "My straw HONKS!" or the tube law: "Longer is lower!"

Out in the real world

Clarinets swing in jazz bands, march in school bands and bark comically in cartoons — and their reed-cousins live in every kitchen drawer: cut a straw’s tip to a point and blow. The woodwind family’s secret costs two cents.

Try it together

Straw-Reed Orchestra: everyone cuts a straw reed. Honk the long straws — deep and silly. Trim them shorter — higher and sillier. Line them up longest to shortest: a straw clarinet choir! Then the long-breath contest: one steady honk, no gulps — who can hold it longest? Steady air is the woodwind superpower, and the straw teaches it for free.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the wooden tongue called? What makes it flutter? Long straw or short — which honks lower?" The reed, your breath, the long one — three answers and the honk is music.

Parent tips

Cut the straw tip for them the first time — two small triangles snipped flat make the reed. And keep honks SHORT in shared rooms; the neighbours will assume a duck has moved in.

This lesson pairs with the Clarinet flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Cymbals — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the cymbals — two golden plates you crash together for the biggest sparkle in music, plus the gentle shimmer that follows every crash like a glitter cloud.

What is this?

Cymbals are two round metal plates: crash them together for a mighty CLANG that rings on and on, or tap and sway one for a shhhimmer. Every drum kit hangs them, every parade carries them.

What does it mean?

The crash is the lesson in big moments: cymbals do not play OFTEN — they play at THE moment, the boom of the story. Choosing WHEN to crash is a whole musical idea: power is about timing, not volume alone.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three cymbal ideas: the crash is edge-to-edge, plates kissing sideways — not face-slam, or the sound chokes; the ring goes on and on after the hands stop — metal remembers; and the shimmer is the gentle version — sway and tremble one cymbal for the soft sparkle.

Why this matters

Cymbals teach restraint-with-power: the child who can HOLD a crash until the big moment has learned musical patience, the rarest skill in any pre-school band.

What it teaches

Edge-alignment striking (a real coordination trick), decay listening (the ring that fades), big-movement control, and the when-to-play decision.

Words to learn

cymbalscrashclangshimmerringmomentsparkle

Say this to your child

“"Cymbals are two golden plates! Bring them together edge to edge — like a crocodile clap — CRASH! And listen: the metal keeps sparkling long after your hands stop. Cymbals do not play all the time — they WAIT for the big moment, the loudest part of the story, and then: CLANG! Waiting well is the cymbal player’s superpower."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "These are cymbals — two golden plates that crash."
  2. The crash secret: plates meet EDGE to edge, like a crocodile clap — sidelong, never face-on. Practise the crocodile clap in the air.
  3. The long ring: crash… and LISTEN — the metal rings after your hands have stopped. Count how long the glitter lasts.
  4. The shimmer: one cymbal, held up, trembling quickly — shhhhhh. The soft sister of the crash.
  5. Play the big-moment game below and close: "wait for the moment, then crash."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Cymbals" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the two plates below — exactly as the golden pair looks.

Ask your child

"How do the plates meet — flat or edge to edge?" "What happens after our hands stop?" "When does a cymbal crash — all the time or at the big moment?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Crocodile clap — CRASH!" "The ring kept going by itself!" or the patient one: "I waited for the big moment!"

Out in the real world

Cymbals crash at every parade, orchestra crescendo and drum-kit fill — and their household cousins hang in every cupboard: two pot lids, edge to edge. The kitchen orchestra’s grand finale, free.

Try it together

Big-Moment Story: tell a tiny story — "and THEN the giant stomped…" — and the cymbalist’s one job is to crash exactly at THEN, not before, not after. Three stories, three crashes, each judged by the room. Then the shimmer: the same cymbalist whispers shhhh under the whole next story. Loud at the moment, soft under the tale — the whole percussion section in one game.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do the plates meet? What keeps sparkling after the crash? What is the soft version?" Edge to edge, the ring, the shimmer — three answers and the moment is ready.

Parent tips

Crocodile clap first, always — face-slams hurt wrists and kill the ring. And honour the wait: a cymbalist who crashes three times in a story gets gently reminded that gold is rare.

This lesson pairs with the Cymbals flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Drum Kit — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the drum kit’s astonishing trick: ONE person plays MANY drums — hands on different drums, feet on others — four body parts telling four rhythm stories at the same time.

What is this?

A drum kit is a whole drum section arranged around one throne: snare between the knees, bass drum under the right foot, toms above, cymbals around — and the drummer plays them all at once.

What does it mean?

The kit is the brain’s greatest rhythm workout: each limb keeps its own pattern while the others keep theirs. Even the beginner version — clap one pattern, tap another — builds the body-splitting that drummers, pianists and typists all share.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three kit ideas: the seat is the centre — everything within arm’s reach and foot’s reach; each limb owns one job — right hand, left hand, right foot, left foot; and the patterns start simple: boom (foot) on one, tap-tap (hands) on four.

Why this matters

Air-drumming a split pattern is the single best pre-instrument exercise there is: the child who can boom-foot while tap-tapping hands has built the coordination every piano and drum lesson will ask for.

What it teaches

Limb independence (the foundation of all kit and keyboard playing), pattern layering, seat-side spatial mapping, and steady beat under physical complexity.

Words to learn

drum kitdrummerthronesnarebass drumpatternlimbs

Say this to your child

“"The drum kit is a whole drum section with ONE player! Sit on the throne — snare between your knees, boom-drum under your foot, cymbals all around. And here is the magic: your hands go tap-tap while your foot goes BOOM — at the same time! Four body parts, four patterns, one drummer. You are the whole band."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a drum kit — many drums, ONE drummer."
  2. The map: name the neighbours — snare between the knees, boom-drum under the foot, cymbals around. Everything close, nothing far.
  3. The split: pat your knees (tap-tap) while stomping one foot (BOOM) — that is already drum-kitting! Hands do tap-tap, foot does BOOM.
  4. Build the home kit: a chair as the throne, a pot (snare), a big box (boom), two lids (cymbals) — the whole section in one corner.
  5. Play the four-limb game below and close: "one drummer, many drums."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Drum Kit" are printed in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the full kit below — drums and cymbals exactly as the set looks.

Ask your child

"How many drummers play a kit? What does the foot play? What do your hands play while the foot booms?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I’m the whole band!" "Tap-tap with my hands, BOOM with my foot!" or the kit-owner’s pride: "My throne is a chair!"

Out in the real world

Drum kits live in every band room and garage — and their four-limb game lives in every car seat: knees patted while feet tap-tap the floor mats. The kit’s brain trick is free to rehearse anywhere.

Try it together

Four-Limb Kit: chair throne, pot snare, box boom, lid cymbals. Level one: hands alternate pot-lid (tap-tap) while the right foot booms the box — thirty seconds, steady. Level two: cymbal crash on your call — "big moment!" — without losing the tap-tap-boom. Level three: swap the boom to the LEFT foot. Every level is the drummer’s real brain-splitter, played at kitchen scale.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many players? Which limbs play what? What do we call the seat?" One, hands-taps and foot-boom, the throne — three answers and the kit is yours.

Parent tips

Start the split with just TWO limbs and add the third only when the first two go steady. And air-drumming counts: steering-wheel kits build exactly this coordination, and nobody has to hear it.

This lesson pairs with the Drum Kit flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Drum — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the drum’s three voices — the big boom, the quick tap, the rumbling roll — and the oldest music game on Earth: I play a rhythm, you answer it.

What is this?

A drum is a skin or membrane stretched tight over a hollow body: strike it with hands or mallets and it speaks. Big hits boom, finger taps patter, and the roll — fast alternating strikes — makes one long thunder.

What does it mean?

The drum is the conversation starter of all music: it asks a rhythm question and waits for an answer. Echo games on a drum are the earliest and best listening training there is — ears first, hands second.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three drum ideas: one drum, many voices — boom (whole hand, big), tap (fingertips, quick), roll (alternating hands, rrrrr); the skin needs to be TIGHT to speak clearly; and the echo is the game — say it back exactly as you heard it.

Why this matters

Drums need no pitch, no notes, no setup — the first instrument and still the fastest way into music. And the echo game builds listening memory that every later melody will borrow.

What it teaches

Striking dynamics (big versus small force), alternating-hand rolls, echo memory (aural working memory), and the discipline of waiting for the question before answering.

Words to learn

drumboomtaprollechorhythmanswer

Say this to your child

“"The drum has three voices! BOOM — the whole hand, big and deep. Tap-tap-tap — fingertips, quick as rain. And rrrrroll — both hands taking turns so fast it becomes one long thunder. And the oldest game in music: I play a rhythm, and YOU answer it back, exactly the same. The drum is the first conversation!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a drum — the first instrument ever, and still the friendliest."
  2. Three voices: BOOM (whole hand, let it sink), tap-tap-tap (fingertips, quick as rain), rrrroll (hands alternating fast — one long thunder). Say each, play each.
  3. Tight skin rule: a floppy drum mumbles — real drums are pulled TIGHT. Tap the card’s drum: tight skin, clear voice.
  4. The echo game: I play two booms — you play two booms. I play tap-tap-boom — you play tap-tap-boom. The drum talks; you answer.
  5. Play the echo game below and close: "boom, tap, roll — and answer back."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Drum" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the drum and its two mallets below — exactly as it looks.

Ask your child

"Name the drum’s three voices. Which voice uses both hands fastest? What do we do after the drum asks a question?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "BOOM, tap, rrrroll!" "I echoed it exactly!" or the leader’s joy: "Now MY rhythm for YOU to answer!"

Out in the real world

Drums open every parade, power every band, and live at home as pots, boxes, overturned buckets and sofa cushions. The echo game needs nothing at all: clap a pattern on your knees — the kitchen is a drum circle.

Try it together

Echo Drum Circle: one pot-drum, two players. The leader plays one bar — boom-boom-tap — and the echoer answers it exactly. Trade the leader crown each round. Then the trick level: leader plays a ROLL — the echoer rolls back. When echoes get perfect, both play TOGETHER — the conversation becomes a duet. That is every drum circle on Earth, at kitchen scale.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the three voices? What does the echo game start with? What makes a roll?" Boom-tap-roll, the drum’s question, hands alternating — three answers and the circle is open.

Parent tips

Model the waiting: the echoer’s hands stay STILL until the question ends — the pause is the listening. And celebrate imperfect echoes warmly: near-misses mean the ears are working exactly hard enough.

This lesson pairs with the Drum flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Flute — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the flute’s gentle secret: no reed, no string — just breath blown across a hole’s edge, split in two, humming. The same magic as blowing across a bottle top.

What is this?

A flute is a long silver tube: blow air ACROSS the mouth-hole (not into it), the breath splits on the edge, and the tube rings with a clear, airy note. Fingers open and close holes along the tube to climb the scale.

What does it mean?

The flute is breath made audible — the most direct instrument there is: your out-breath, singing. Edge-blowing is a small physical marvel (aim too low and it’s silent, too high and it’s just wind), and bottles teach it free.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three flute ideas: the breath goes ACROSS the hole, not into it — like blowing across a bottle top; the edge splits the breath and half of it hums; and long songs need long breath — flutists are the great breath-savers.

Why this matters

Bottle-blowing is the cheapest lab in music: aim, adjust, hum. A child who coaxes a note from a bottle has genuinely played a flute’s physics — and learned that tiny aim-changes change everything.

What it teaches

Directed breath control (the aim is a fine-motor skill of the lips), sustained out-breath, cause-and-effect micro-adjustment, and soft dynamics — the flute whispers before it sings.

Words to learn

flutebreathedgeblow acrossbottlesilveraim

Say this to your child

“"The flute is breath turned to silver! No reed, no strings — you just blow GENTLY ACROSS the hole, like cooling soup, and the edge splits your breath: half flies away, half hums inside the tube — and the tube SINGS. Try it on a bottle tonight: across the top, softly… there it is. Your own breath, turned into music."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a flute — breath made of silver."
  2. The across trick: pretend to cool soup — blow GENTLY ACROSS, not down. The flute’s mouth-hole works the same way: across the edge, never into the hole.
  3. Bottle lab: an empty bottle, blow gently across its top — fwoo! A note! Tilt the aim up and down until it hums clear. That hunting IS flute-playing.
  4. The water trick: pour a little water in — the note DROPS lower. Bottle flutes tune themselves.
  5. Play the breath game below and close: "across the edge, gently."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Flute" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the silver flute below — exactly as the long tube looks.

Ask your child

"Which way does the breath go — into the hole or across it? What happens if we blow too hard? What does water in the bottle do to the note?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Across, like cooling soup!" "My bottle sang!" or the flutist’s discovery: "Gentle works — big blows are just wind!"

Out in the real world

Flutes are the world’s oldest instruments — bone flutes are forty thousand years old — and they live in every orchestra, band and school hall. Their bottles sit in every recycling bin: free flutes, waiting.

Try it together

Bottle Flute Choir: three bottles, water at three levels — low, middle, high. Hunt each note with gentle across-breath, then play calls: leader "sings" two bottle notes, echoer answers. Finish with the breath-length contest: one steady bottle note, no wobble — the longest gentle breath wins. Silver-song physics, at recycling prices.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which way does breath cross the hole? What splits the breath? What makes the bottle note lower?" Across, the edge, more water — three answers and the breath is silver.

Parent tips

Gentle is the whole game — model soup-cooling breath and the note arrives in seconds. And let the aim-hunt take its time: the searching IS the lesson; the note is the receipt.

This lesson pairs with the Flute flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

French Horn — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the French horn — brass wound into a great coil, played with a hand tucked inside the bell, making the roundest, mellowest hoot in the whole brass family.

What is this?

A French horn is brass tubing coiled into a big circle, ending in a wide flaring bell: buzz the mouthpiece, and the long coiled tube hums a noble, mellow note — with the right hand tucked inside the bell to shape it.

What does it mean?

The coil is the lesson: the horn’s tube is SO long (unrolled, over four metres) that it must spiral to stay playable — and long tube means low, warm, rich. Length is tone: the horn’s snail-shell is its sound.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three horn ideas: the tube is coiled because it is ENORMOUS — unrolled, longer than a car; the hand rests inside the bell like a mute pillow, softening the sound; and the horn’s voice is the mellow one — round where the trumpet is bright.

Why this matters

The horn teaches tube-length thinking — the law behind every brass and woodwind instrument — and its tucked hand is the friendliest reminder that players shape sound with their whole body.

What it teaches

Length-pitch mapping, buzz control (lip buzzing is the brass engine), mellow-versus-bright listening, and the gentle-hand shaping idea.

Words to learn

French horncoilbellhandmellowbrasstube

Say this to your child

“"The French horn is a snail-shell of brass! Its tube is so long it has to coil — unrolled, longer than a car! — and long tubes hum deep and warm. The player buzzes their lips into the mouthpiece — brrr! — and tucks one hand inside the big bell, like a soft pillow, to make the hoot round and mellow. The gentlest giant in the brass family."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the French horn — a very long tube, coiled like a snail shell."
  2. The coil: trace the spiral on the card with a finger — round and round. Unrolled, this tube is longer than a car! Long tube = deep, warm hoot.
  3. The bell hand: the right hand tucks INSIDE the wide bell — a soft pillow that rounds the sound. Tuck a hand over a cup’s mouth and hum: warmer, rounder. That is the horn hand.
  4. Buzz the engine: lips together, blow a raspberry — brrr. That lip buzz is what every brass instrument plays. The horn just makes it noble.
  5. Play the mellow game below and close: "long coil, warm hoot."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "French Horn" stand in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration below — the coiled brass and its wide bell exactly as the horn looks.

Ask your child

"Why does the horn coil? Where does the hand go? Which is mellow — the horn or the bright trumpet?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The tube is longer than a car!" "My hand is the sound pillow!" or the buzz report: "Brrr — my lips are the engine!"

Out in the real world

Horns call across every orchestra’s back row — hunting calls, film fanfares — and the coil law lives at home: a garden hose coiled on its hook is a French horn’s twin. Unroll the hose, drop the pitch: length is tone.

Try it together

Mellow-or-Bright: two players hum the same note — one through a cup (bright, forward), one with a hand-pillow over the cup’s mouth (mellow, round). The room votes on which is the horn and which the trumpet. Then the coil law: hum through a rolled poster (long tube) — deep! Hum through a short straw — high! The horn’s snail-shell, understood by lunchtime.

Understanding check

Ask: "Why coil the tube? What does the hand in the bell do? What kind of voice does the horn have?" It is very long, softens and rounds it, mellow — three answers and the horn hoots.

Parent tips

Buzzing lips IS brass — practise the raspberry proudly; it is the engine, not a joke. And the cup-and-hand demo is the horn’s whole personality: try it before explaining it.

This lesson pairs with the French Horn flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Gong — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the gong’s luxurious idea: one gentle strike, and the sound keeps blooming for a whole minute — music you mostly LISTEN to, with your hands in your lap.

What is this?

A gong is a big round metal disc hanging from a frame: strike it softly with a large soft mallet and it swells — ooooooom — ringing, shifting and fading for up to a minute. It opens concerts, closes ceremonies, settles whole rooms.

What does it mean?

Every other instrument asks the player to keep playing. The gong asks the player to STOP: one touch, then hands still, ears open. It is the shelf’s meditation cushion — the instrument that teaches listening by demanding nothing else.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three gong ideas: the mallet is big and SOFT — a hard stick chokes the bloom; the sound GROWS after the strike (swell) and fades like a slow sunset; and the game is stillness — one strike, then how long can we simply listen?

Why this matters

In a room of tap-tap-boom, the gong is the one instrument that rewards quiet hands and patient ears — and children who learn the gong’s stillness carry that stillness into every other loud day.

What it teaches

Decay listening (a full minute of one sound changing), soft-force striking, stillness stamina, and swell-shape awareness — sound that grows, peaks and fades.

Words to learn

gongstrikemalletswellringfadestillness

Say this to your child

“"The gong is the gentlest giant! One soft touch with the big soft mallet — oooooom — and the sound blooms: it grows… and grows… and slowly, slowly fades away, like a sunset. And our job? Strike ONCE, put our hands in our laps, and LISTEN with our whole bodies. The gong plays; we wonder."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a gong — one touch, one minute of shimmer."
  2. The soft rule: the gong is struck with a big soft mallet — like patting a giant’s shoulder, never punching it. Soft touch, giant voice.
  3. The swell: strike… and wait — the sound GROWS before it fades. A slow sunrise, then a slow sunset: that is a gong’s whole day.
  4. The stillness: strike once, hands in lap — how long can we listen? Breathe with the gong.
  5. Play the listening game below and close: "one strike, big ears."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Gong" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the big round gong below — exactly as it hangs.

Ask your child

"What kind of mallet does the gong like — hard stick or soft? Does the sound stop right away? What do OUR hands do after the strike?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Soft pat — giant voice!" "The sound grew, then faded!" or the still one: "I listened for the whole sunset."

Out in the real world

Gongs open boxing matches, close yoga classes and hum under every mysterious film scene — and their bloom lives at home: a struck metal bowl, a fence post, even a wet finger on a wineglass rim. Slow sound is everywhere.

Try it together

Gong Listening: a metal bowl or pot-lid with a sock mallet. One strike — everyone still — listen until EVERYONE agrees the sound is truly gone (it lasts longer than anyone guesses). Three strikes, three silences. Then the reverse game: the "gongist" strikes at a secret moment during quiet breathing — ears open, eyes closed — who heard the bloom start? Stillness becomes the sport.

Understanding check

Ask: "What kind of touch does the gong want? What does the sound do after the strike? What do our hands do?" Soft, swells and fades, rest in our laps — three answers and the room goes still.

Parent tips

The sock mallet and the stillness rule are the lesson — soft strike, still hands. And let the "is it gone yet?" debate run: arguing about the last whisper of a ring is genuine listening, wearing pyjamas.

This lesson pairs with the Gong flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Guitar — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the guitar — six strings on a big wooden body, the instrument that can strum a campfire song or pick a lullaby, and the one every child already owns in shoebox form.

What is this?

A guitar is a string instrument with a big waisted body and six strings: strum them all with a sweep for big chords, pick them one by one for melodies, and press strings against the frets to change notes.

What does it mean?

The guitar is two instruments in one: the strum (all strings, one heartbeat — the campfire) and the pick (one string, one note — the melody). Naming that split early gives every future player their two first skills.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three guitar ideas: strum = all six at once, one big sweep; pick = one string, one note; the frets are the ladder — press a string down at a higher fret, the note climbs. And the body is the drum of it: the big wooden box is why guitars sound warm.

Why this matters

The guitar is the world’s most-played instrument for a reason a four-year-old can already touch: one sweep = instant song. And the shoebox version is the classic first build for exactly that reason.

What it teaches

Strum-vs-pick contrast, fret-ladder pitch thinking, one-finger chording on rubber bands, and strumming steady while singing — the two-track skill.

Words to learn

guitarstringsstrumpickfretschordbody

Say this to your child

“"The guitar has two voices! Strum — one big sweep across ALL six strings, swish, that is the heartbeat of the campfire song. Pick — one finger, one string, pling, that is the little tune on top. And the stairs up the neck — the frets — let your fingers climb the notes. Every campfire you will ever sit at has one of these in the middle."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a guitar — six strings and a big wooden voice."
  2. The two jobs: strum (whole hand sweeps all the strings — swish!) and pick (one finger, one string — pling!). Do both in the air, then on the card.
  3. The fret ladder: the metal strips along the neck are steps — press a string behind a higher fret and the note climbs. Frets are the guitar’s stairs.
  4. Shoebox guitar: rubber bands around a tissue box, paper-towel-roll neck taped on — strum it: instant campfire.
  5. Play the two-jobs game below and close: "strum the heart, pick the tune."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Guitar" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the guitar below — the strings and body exactly as the instrument looks.

Ask your child

"What is one big sweep across all the strings called? One string, one note? What do we press to climb the notes?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Strum is swish, pick is pling!" "The frets are stairs!" or the builder’s pride: "My shoebox has a paper-towel neck!"

Out in the real world

Guitars sit in every living room, classroom and campfire circle on Earth — and their shoebox twins are every childhood’s first build. Strum one today; the swish is instant.

Try it together

Two-Jobs Band: box guitar ready. The leader calls "STRUM!" — one big sweep. "PICK!" — one careful pling. Then mix: "strum… strum… pick-pick… STRUM!" The player follows; the listener dances. Then the campfire finish: everyone strums a steady swish-swish while one song is sung together. Six strings, one heartbeat.

Understanding check

Ask: "All six strings at once is called? One string alone? What are the stairs on the neck?" A strum, a pick, the frets — three answers and the campfire is lit.

Parent tips

Rubber bands with different thicknesses make different plings — let the child tune their shoebox by ear. And keep strums slow and proud: a steady swish beats a wild flail every time.

This lesson pairs with the Guitar flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Harmonica — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the harmonica’s two-way secret: blow OUT for one note, breathe IN for another — the only instrument on the shelf that plays on the inhale, and small enough to live in a pocket.

What is this?

A harmonica is a tiny bar of metal combs and reeds: blow through a hole and one reed sings; breathe IN through the same hole and a different reed answers. Ten holes, twenty notes, whole songs — and it fits in a sock drawer.

What does it mean?

The blow-draw pair is a breathing revelation: music on the EXHALE and the INHALE. Children discover their own breath has two directions of song — and the harmonica’s size makes it the first instrument that goes everywhere they do.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three harmonica ideas: blow = one note, draw (breathe in) = a different note — the two are neighbours on every hole; it moves ACROSS the lips — tilt and slide to find holes; and the train sound — two notes chuffing in and out — is the famous first song.

Why this matters

The blow-draw game trains breath direction awareness that swimming, woodwinds and singing all borrow later — and the harmonica hands it over in a toy-sized, pocket-sized, giggle-sized package.

What it teaches

Bidirectional breath control, small-muscle slide-and-tilt, pattern pairs (blow-draw-blow), and the confidence of carrying an instrument in a pocket.

Words to learn

harmonicablowdrawbreathe inholesslidechuff

Say this to your child

“"The harmonica plays on BOTH breaths! Blow OUT — one note. Breathe IN — a different note! It tilts against your lips, and sliding along finds new holes: wee-oo-wee-oo. And the famous first song is a train: chuffa-chuffa, out and in, out and in — a whole railway in your pocket!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a harmonica — a whole band in your pocket."
  2. The two ways: blow OUT through a hole — one note. Breathe IN through the same hole — a different note! The harmonica plays both ways; no other shelf instrument does.
  3. The slide: it rests against the lips and TILTS — moving mouth finds moving holes. Slide gently along: wee-oo-wee-oo.
  4. The train: blow-draw-blow-draw on two neighbouring holes — chuffa-chuffa — the famous harmonica train.
  5. Play the train game below and close: "out and in, both directions sing."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Harmonica" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the small harmonica below — exactly as the pocket band looks.

Ask your child

"What do we call breathing IN on the harmonica? What happens on the same hole when we draw? What is the famous first song?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Blow and draw — two notes, one hole!" "Wee-oo — I’m sliding!" or the chuff: "Chuffa-chuffa — my train!"

Out in the real world

Harmonicas ride in pockets everywhere — folk, blues, campfires — and the blow-draw trick lives in every blade of grass held between thumbs and every bottle-top whistle. Breath both ways is an old, old human toy.

Try it together

Pocket Train: harmonica (or paper-tube stand-in). Find one blow note, one draw note — neighbours. Chuff them in a slow rhythm: out-in, out-in — the train leaves the station! Speed up gently… round the mountain… slow to a stop at the platform. Then the echo game: two notes blown, two drawn — answered. Twenty notes, one pocket, whole journeys.

Understanding check

Ask: "What note plays when we breathe IN? How does the mouth find new holes? What is the first song?" A draw note, by sliding, the train — three answers and the pocket sings.

Parent tips

Tilting works better than pushing — the harmonica rests on the lips like a feather. And keep it personal: harmonicas are one-mouth instruments; every player deserves their own (even if the paper tube gets the encore).

This lesson pairs with the Harmonica flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Harp — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the harp — the tall instrument where the strings stand in a ladder: long strings at your tummy ring low, short strings above ring high, and one sweep makes the famous angel-run.

What is this?

A harp is a frame of strings standing upright: nearly fifty of them, arranged long to short. Pluck a string and it sings one soft note; drag a finger across all of them — the glissando — and the whole sky ripples at once.

What does it mean?

The harp makes pitch VISIBLE in the most beautiful way: string length IS the ladder. Long-low at the bottom, short-high at the top — the whole scale standing upright in golden rows, pluckable by anyone.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three harp ideas: long string = low note, short string = high note — the ladder stands upright here; the pluck is gentle — pull-and-release like picking an apple, never a snap; and the glissando is one finger dragging across ALL the strings — the angel run.

Why this matters

The glissando is the most beautiful one-finger sound in music — instant, enormous, achievable on day one. And the length-pitch ladder repeats later on every stringed instrument a child will meet.

What it teaches

Length-pitch mapping (upright this time), gentle pluck-release control, the sweeping glissando, and high-low ordering across nearly fifty choices.

Words to learn

harpstringsladderpluckglissandolongshort

Say this to your child

“"The harp is a ladder of strings standing up to the sky! Long strings at the bottom — low and sleepy. Short strings at the top — high and sparkly. Pluck one like picking an apple: pling. And drag one finger across ALL of them — fwwwish! — the glissando, the angel run, the most beautiful sweep in music."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a harp — a ladder of strings standing up to the sky."
  2. The upright ladder: strings at the bottom are LONG — low, sleepy. Strings at the top are SHORT — high, sparkly. The scale is standing up!
  3. The apple pluck: pull the string gently and let go — like picking an apple, soft and round. Never a sharp snap.
  4. The glissando: one finger, dragging slowly across ALL the strings — fwwwwwish! The angel run. Practise slow, then slower.
  5. Play the ladder game below and close: "long is low, short is high."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Harp" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the tall harp below — its strings exactly as the ladder looks.

Ask your child

"Which strings ring low — long or short? What is the gentle pluck like? What do we call dragging one finger across all the strings?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Long is low, short is high!" "The apple pluck!" or the angel run: "Fwwwish — I played the whole sky!"

Out in the real world

Harps stand in orchestras, Irish pubs and storybooks of angels — and their ladder lives on every rubber-band frame and garden fence: long band low, short band high. The angel run is one finger away.

Try it together

Rubber-Band Harp Ladder: stretch five bands of different lengths over an open box or chair back — long to short, bottom to top. Pluck the ladder: low… high. Name it, then sing it. Then the glissando: one finger, one slow sweep — the room fills. Finish with harp stories: every sparkle moment in a fairy film is this exact sweep. Now it lives at your house.

Understanding check

Ask: "Long string or short — which is low? What is the gentle pluck called here? What is the sweep?" Long-low, the apple pluck, the glissando — three answers and the ladder sings.

Parent tips

Different band lengths AND thicknesses both change pitch — let the child rebuild the ladder until the order sings true. And the apple pluck keeps fingers (and bands) safe from snapping.

This lesson pairs with the Harp flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Maracas — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the maracas — two gourds of rattling seeds that speak in shakes: big shake, small shake, and the secret third sound, the still-and-silent one.

What is this?

Maracas are shakers: dried gourds (or any hollow shell) holding seeds or beads — shake once and they rattle, hold still and they hush. Latin American music leans on them, and every kitchen owns their cousins.

What does it mean?

The maracas’ third sound is the lesson: STOPPING is part of rhythm. Shake-shake-REST — the silence between shakes is as musical as the rattle. Children who can hold a still maracas have found rhythm’s quiet half.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three maracas ideas: the shake comes from the WRIST — a flick, not a whole-arm windmill; three sounds exist — big shake, small shake, stillness; and patterns make sentences: shake-shake-still, shake-shake-still.

Why this matters

Wrist-shaking builds the small-motor beat that claves, castanets and drum kits all ask for — and the stillness pattern teaches the rest note, the skill every ensemble player needs and few beginners own.

What it teaches

Wrist-flick control, pattern memory with rests, loud-soft dynamics in one hand, and ensemble stillness — shaking together, stopping together.

Words to learn

maracasshakerattlewriststillpatternrest

Say this to your child

“"Maracas are gourds full of seeds — and they talk in shakes! Flick from the wrist: chh! Big shake for the loud part, small shake for the soft part… and the secret third sound: STILLNESS. Hands frozen, not a peep. Shake, shake, still… shake, shake, still — the silence is part of the song!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "These are maracas — gourds of rattling seeds."
  2. The wrist flick: hold the arm still, flick the wrist — chh. Small move, big sound. Windmilling arms are tiring; wrist flicks go all night.
  3. Three sounds: BIG shake (chh!), small shake (chh), and STILL — hands frozen, silence. All three are music.
  4. Build home maracas: rice or beans in a bottle or egg cup, lid taped — a family band’s worth in five minutes.
  5. Play the freeze game below and close: "shake, shake, still."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Maracas" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the pair below — exactly as the rattling gourds look.

Ask your child

"Where does the shake come from — the arm or the wrist? What is the maracas’ third sound? What goes inside a home-made pair?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Wrist flick — chh!" "Stillness is a sound too!" or the builder’s pride: "My bottle has rice in it — shake!"

Out in the real world

Maracas drive salsa, samba and every Latin beach song — and their cousins rattle in every kitchen: rice in a bottle, beads in a tin, a pill box of pasta. The wrist flick costs nothing.

Try it together

Freeze-Shake: everyone shakes a steady wrist-flick beat — chh-chh-chh — until the leader calls FREEZE! Total stillness, no single rattle. Restart on the clap. Then patterns: "shake-shake-still" in unison — a whole band silent on the same beat is the game’s magic. Shake together, stop together: that is an orchestra’s discipline in a bottle of rice.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the flick live? Name the three sounds. What freezes on FREEZE?" The wrist, big-small-still, everything — three answers and the band is steady.

Parent tips

The freeze is the point — praise the silent freeze louder than the shake. And rice-before-beans: rice rattles softer and sweeps up easier.

This lesson pairs with the Maracas flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Microphone — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the microphone’s friendly contract: it lifts your voice — but it also broadcasts every giggle and whisper, so the star’s job is calm breath and a steady mouth.

What is this?

A microphone turns sound waves into tiny electrical signals, sends them to a speaker, and the speaker plays them back BIG. Singers, reporters and radio hosts all speak into one — softly, and close.

What does it mean?

The microphone rewards the small voice: whisper into it and the room hears you; shout into it and the speakers shout back, distorted and grumpy. Quiet-in, big-out is the whole technique — power comes from the machine, not the throat.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three microphone ideas: hold it a hand’s width from the mouth — close enough to catch, far enough to breathe; do NOT shout — the speakers do the shouting; and keep it steady — wobbling microphones make wobbling sound.

Why this matters

Speaking into a microphone is a confidence skill every school assembly eventually asks for — and learning it as a game, at four, with a toilet-roll mic, makes the real one feel like an old friend.

What it teaches

Voice modulation (soft in, big out), distance awareness, steady-hand holding, and performance confidence — announcing to a room is brave, and games make it safe.

Words to learn

microphonespeakeramplifywhisperannouncesteadyvoice

Say this to your child

“"The microphone is the voice-lifter! Speak SOFTLY into it — the speaker does the shouting for you. Hold it a hand’s width from your mouth, steady like an ice-cream cone, and announce: GOOD MORNING, EVERYONE! Your whisper, the room’s giant — that is the microphone’s magic."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a microphone — the voice-lifter!"
  2. The contract: it makes SMALL voices BIG. So the trick is: speak SOFTLY into it, and let the speaker do the shouting.
  3. The distance: a hand’s width from the mouth. Too far — the sound hides; touching the lips — the speakers go BOOM and grumble. Hand’s width is just right.
  4. The steady hold: one hand, cupped loosely, mic like an ice-cream cone — no wobbling, no swinging.
  5. Play the announcer game below and close: "soft in, big out."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Microphone" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a smiling microphone illustration below and music notes around it — exactly as the voice-lifter looks.

Ask your child

"Should we shout into the microphone or whisper? How far from the mouth? What does the speaker do with our small voice?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Soft in, big out!" "A hand’s width away!" or the star’s line: "GOOD MORNING, EVERYONE!"

Out in the real world

Microphones stand in every school hall, radio station and stage — and their game-twin is every toilet roll and hairbrush on Earth. Announce into one tonight: the confidence transfers word for word.

Try it together

The Announcer: a toilet-roll "mic," held a hand’s width away, steady. Announcements in your softest voice: "WELCOME TO DINNER!" "THE SOAP IS… SOAPY!" The "speaker" (a partner) repeats it back at giant volume with cupped hands around their mouth. Whisper in, giant out — the whole broadcast chain, played by two people.

Understanding check

Ask: "Shout or whisper in? How far from the mouth? What does the speaker do?" Whisper, a hand’s width, shouts it back — three answers and the show is on.

Parent tips

Model the too-close boom once — the grumpy speaker sound teaches distance faster than any rule. And praise steady hands over loud voices: the mic does the volume; the star does the calm.

This lesson pairs with the Microphone flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Stage Microphone — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the stage microphone — the handheld singer’s mic that tilts, pulls away on the big notes, and comes with its own manners: thank the crowd, share the stage.

What is this?

The stage microphone is the handheld kind singers grab: held at the chin, tilted for high notes, pulled away for the loudest ones so the speakers do not shout. It lives on a stand between songs and waits its turn.

What does it mean?

The stage mic adds performance craft to the microphone’s physics: the PULL-AWAY on big notes (the pro move), the tilt that shapes the sound, and the manners — the mic is shared, the crowd is thanked, the stage is a kind place.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three stage-mic ideas: hold it at the chin, not the lips — singing needs jaw room; PULL it away on the very biggest notes — let the speakers finish the shout; and between songs it rests on the stand — the mic waits its turn like everyone on stage.

Why this matters

Stage craft — where to stand, when to pull, how to thank — is the part of music no textbook teaches late. Playing it at four, with a hairbrush, builds performers who are generous on real stages.

What it teaches

Performance gestures (tilt, pull-away), breath-and-jaw awareness at the chin, turn-taking on stage, and crowd manners — the bow, the thank-you.

Words to learn

stagehandheldchintiltpull awaystandcrowd

Say this to your child

“"The stage mic is the singer’s friend! Hold it at your chin — your jaw needs room to sing. Tilt it a little for the high notes… and on the BIGGEST note of all — pull it away! Let the speakers finish the shout. Then back on the stand it goes, waiting its turn. And at the end: bow, and thank the crowd — that is stage manners."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the stage microphone — the singer’s mic, the one stars grab and tilt."
  2. The chin hold: mic at the CHIN, not squashing the lips — singers need their jaws free to open wide.
  3. The pull-away: on the biggest, loudest note — pull the mic AWAY! The speakers finish the shout. That is the pro move; practise it on one giant note.
  4. The stand rest: between songs the mic goes back on its stand — everyone on stage waits their turn, even the mic.
  5. Play the stage game below and close: "chin, tilt, pull away — and thank the crowd."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Microphone" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a yellow handheld stage microphone illustrated below — exactly as the stage star’s tool looks.

Ask your child
