"Where does the stage mic rest — lips or chin? What do we do on the biggest note? Where does the mic wait between songs?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Chin, not lips!" "Pull away on the BIG one!" or the star’s manners: "Thank you, crowd — good night!"

Out in the real world

Stage mics tilt and pull away in every concert film and talent show — watch one chorus closely and catch the pull-away on the high note. The move is everywhere once your eyes know it.

Try it together

The Star’s Set: hairbrush mic, sofa-arm stage. One song — hummed or sung — with the three pro moves: chin hold, tilt on the highs, PULL-AWAY on the giant finish. The crowd (everyone else) goes wild. Then the manners: mic to the stand, bow, "THANK YOU!" — and the next star gets the stage. Everyone performs, everyone claps: that is show business, four years old.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the mic rest while singing? What is the move on the biggest note? What do we do at the end?" At the chin, pull away, bow and thank — three answers and the stage is yours.

Parent tips

The pull-away is the star of the lesson — one giant note, one dramatic pull, guaranteed laughter. And rotate the stage fast: short sets, big applause, generous crowds.

This lesson pairs with the Stage Microphone flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Oboe — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the oboe’s double secret: TWO reeds strapped together, buzzing against each other — the duck-voiced woodwind that the entire orchestra listens to when it tunes.

What is this?

An oboe is a slender black tube with a DOUBLE reed: two thin blades of cane bound face to face. Blow and the blades flutter against each other — a bright, nasal, penetrating voice. Orchestras tune to the oboe’s long-held A.

What does it mean?

The oboe’s voice is unmistakable — duck-call bright — and its job is trust: when the oboe plays its A, a hundred musicians tune to ONE note. The brightest squawk in the room becomes the standard everyone agrees on.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three oboe ideas: TWO reeds, face to face — the flutter happens between them, reed on reed; the voice is bright and nasal — a duck with excellent manners; and the orchestra’s tuning note is the oboe’s long, steady A — the most-listened-to note in classical music.

Why this matters

The double reed doubles the straw-clarinet idea (two blades, not one), and the tuning ritual teaches something bigger: a whole team agreeing on one sound, started by one small, bright voice.

What it teaches

Double-vibration thinking, bright-versus-warm tone listening, the tuning ritual — steady pitch as a team standard — and fine breath pressure for a delicate reed.

Words to learn

oboedouble reedtwo bladesbrighttuneAorchestra

Say this to your child

“"The oboe has TWO reeds — two thin wooden blades strapped face to face! Blow between them and they flutter against each other: reed-on-reed — a bright, duckish voice. And here is its great job: before a concert, the oboe plays one long, steady A — and the WHOLE orchestra tunes to it. The brightest squawk becomes the note everyone trusts."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is an oboe — the woodwind with TWO reeds kissing."
  2. The double: the clarinet has one reed; the oboe has TWO thin blades bound face to face — they flutter AGAINST each other. Two tongues, one quack.
  3. Straw demo: flatten a straw tip, cut TWO small blades, blow — the double-reed honk! Compare with a single-blade straw: double is brighter.
  4. The A ritual: the oboe plays one long, steady A — and the whole orchestra listens and matches it. Steady is the whole job.
  5. Play the tuning game below and close: "two reeds, one A."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Oboe" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the oboe and its reed below — exactly as the slender tube looks.

Ask your child

"How many reeds does the oboe have? Which bird does it sound a little like? What note does the orchestra tune to?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "TWO reeds, kissing!" "A duck with manners!" or the tuner’s pride: "My long A is the boss note!"

Out in the real world

Oboes sit centre-stage at every orchestra’s tuning — listen for the lone A before the concert: that is the oboe, and a hundred instruments agreeing with it. The double reed lives at home too: two flattened straw blades will honk it.

Try it together

Tune the Orchestra: one player is the OBOE — hums one long, steady AHHH. Everyone else is the orchestra: one by one, they join the SAME pitch until the room hums as one note. Wobbly joiners get the oboe’s frown; steady ones the nod. Then the concert begins — one note, a hundred players, zero squawks. That is the oboe’s real job, rehearsed.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many reeds? What do they do to each other? What is the oboe’s big job before a concert?" Two, flutter against each other, give the tuning A — three answers and the orchestra can begin.

Parent tips

Two blades beat one for the demo — the between-reeds flutter is the whole physics. And praise STEADY over loud: the oboe’s A is honoured for its evenness, not its volume.

This lesson pairs with the Oboe flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Piano — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the piano’s grand idea: eighty-eight keys laid out in one perfect ladder — low on the left, high on the right — and inside every key, a little hammer waiting to strike a string.

What is this?

A piano is a keyboard over hammers and strings: press a key, a felt hammer strikes a string inside, and the note rings. The keys run low (left) to high (right), with the black keys standing in twos and threes like landmarks.

What does it mean?

The piano is the pitch ladder made physical: every note has its own key, in order, waiting. No breath, no bow, no tuning — just reach, press, hear. It is the clearest map of music ever built, and children read it by walking it.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three piano ideas: left is LOW, right is HIGH — the ladder lies flat under your fingers; inside each key a hammer strikes a string — the piano is a drum shop for strings; and the black keys are landmarks — two-then-three, two-then-three — the map’s signposts.

Why this matters

Key-order thinking — one note per key, left-low right-high — is the foundation every keyboard, glockenspiel and scale climbs. And the hammer-inside story turns pressing into a small mechanical joy.

What it teaches

Pitch mapping across space (left-right ladder), one-finger pressing to five-finger walking, pattern spotting (the black-key groups), and the cause-press-effect-sound loop.

Words to learn

pianokeyshammerstringlowhighblack keys

Say this to your child

“"The piano is eighty-eight keys in one long ladder! Left side — big, sleepy, LOW notes. Right side — tiny, sparkly, HIGH notes. And here is the secret inside: press a key and a little hammer strikes a string — bonk! — the piano is a drum shop for strings. Find the black keys: two… three… two… three — the mountains that show you where you are."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a piano — eighty-eight keys, one long ladder."
  2. The ladder law: slide a finger along the card’s keyboard left to right — the notes climb. Left: big sleepy notes. Right: tiny sparkly ones.
  3. The hammer story: press a key and inside, a little felt hammer strikes a string — bonk! The piano is a room full of tiny drummers with tiny drums.
  4. Black-key landmarks: find the groups — two… three… two… three. The black keys are the keyboard’s mountains: they never change their pattern.
  5. Play the ladder games below and close: "left is low, right is high."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Piano" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly toy-piano illustration below — its keys exactly as the ladder looks.

Ask your child

"Which side is low — left or right? What strikes the string inside? What pattern do the black keys make?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Left is low, right is high!" "A little hammer — bonk!" or the map-reader: "Two, three, two, three — the black mountains!"

Out in the real world

Pianos stand in every school hall and living room — and their ladder lives on every toy keyboard, tablet app and drawn-on-paper eight-key strip. The hammer story works on all of them: press, bonk, hear.

Try it together

Paper-Key Ladder: draw eight keys on paper — white row with black groups — and "play" the ladder with one finger, low to high, humming each step. Then the landmark hunt: caller says "find a two-group!" — finger lands on it. Finish with the high-low guessing game: player presses a mystery key (or hums a mystery note) — the other calls LOW or HIGH. Eighty-eight keys, one flat ladder, fully walked.

Understanding check

Ask: "Left or right for the low notes? What is inside every key? What do the black keys mark?" Left, a hammer, the map’s groups — three answers and the ladder is walked.

Parent tips

Paper keys first: the left-right law is spatial, and drawing it cements it. And always touch-name the black-key groups before playing melodies — landmarks first, roads after.

This lesson pairs with the Piano flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Piccolo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the piccolo — the flute’s tiny half-sister — and the law it proves: make the tube half as long and the song jumps an octave higher. Small pipe, giant sparkle.

What is this?

A piccolo is a flute shrunk to half its length: same shape, same edge-blowing, but the notes ring an octave higher — so bright and piercing that one piccolo can be heard over a hundred-piece marching band.

What does it mean?

The piccolo is the length-pitch law at its most dramatic: half the tube, double the speed of the sound-waves, one whole octave up. And its job is the sparkle — the star-shriek above the parade that every ear finds first.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three piccolo ideas: it is a HALF-size flute — same blow, shorter tube; half the length sings a whole octave higher — the small-equals-high law at full power; and its voice is the sparkle that floats OVER the whole band.

Why this matters

The octave jump is one of music’s deepest patterns, and the piccolo-flute pair shows it physically: two instruments, same shape, one octave apart. Size-pitch has never been easier to see and hear.

What it teaches

Length-octave mapping, bright-vs-warm tone spotting, listening for one voice inside many (auditory figure-ground), and the piccolo’s proud smallness.

Words to learn

piccolooctavehalf sizehighsparklebandbright

Say this to your child

“"The piccolo is a flute cut in HALF — same shape, half the length — and here is the magic: half the tube makes the song jump a WHOLE octave higher! It is the smallest pipe in the band with the biggest sparkle: listen to a marching band and find it — flying over the drums, over the brass, over everything. Small instrument, giant voice!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a piccolo — the flute’s tiny half-sister."
  2. The half law: lay the card’s piccolo beside the flute card’s memory — half the length! And the song jumps a whole octave higher. Small pipe, big sparkle.
  3. The sparkle job: play a marching-band video — find the piccolo flying OVER everything. One small pipe, heard over a hundred instruments.
  4. Octave hum: hum a note, then hum the SAME note higher — same song, smaller — that is what the piccolo does to the flute’s every note.
  5. Play the sparkle game below and close: "half the size, an octave higher."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Piccolo" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the small piccolo below — exactly as the tiny flute looks.

Ask your child

"How long is a piccolo next to a flute? What happens to the notes? Which voice does your ear find first in a band?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Half the flute, an octave higher!" "The sparkle on top!" or the humming one: "Same song, smaller!"

Out in the real world

Piccolos lead every marching band and military parade — and the octave law lives on every keyboard: press a key, press its twin far right — same note, smaller. Small equals high, everywhere.

Try it together

Octave Twins: hum a simple three-note song. Now hum it an octave higher — the piccolo’s job. Then the band game: everyone drums a steady beat (the band), while the "piccolo" sings the three-note song ON TOP, twice as small and bright. Find-the-sparkle round: eyes closed, one voice sings above the pat-pat — which note? Half-size pipes, fully heard.

Understanding check

Ask: "How does the piccolo compare to a flute? What does half the tube do to the notes? What is its job in the band?" Half the length, an octave higher, the sparkle on top — three answers and the sparkle is caught.

Parent tips

Humming the octave is tricky and thrilling — let the child slide up until it feels "the same but tiny." That same-but-smaller feeling IS an octave, understood by body.

This lesson pairs with the Piccolo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Recorder — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the recorder — the instrument millions of children play first — with its two golden rules: gentle breath, sealed holes. Three notes by Friday, guaranteed.

What is this?

A recorder is a slim plastic (or wooden) tube with a whistle mouth and finger holes: breathe gently into the mouthpiece and cover the holes in patterns to play. Its first three notes — B, A, G — are the doorway to a hundred songs.

What does it mean?

The recorder is the great first instrument because it is honest physics: cover the holes fully and it sings; leak one and it squeaks. Fingering discipline, breath control and immediate music — all in a two-dollar tube.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three recorder ideas: gentle breath — a soft "too," never a hurricane (hurricanes squeak); holes are SEALED with finger pads, flat and full, no leaks; and the first ladder: all fingers down is one note, lift one finger for the next — holes are the ladder’s rungs.

Why this matters

Hole-covering is the finger-and-breath handshake every woodwind asks for, learned here on the friendliest tube ever made. And the three-note repertoire means real songs in the first week.

What it teaches

Finger-pad sealing (a genuine fine-motor milestone), gentle breath control, hole-ladder sequencing, and the first real melodies by finger order.

Words to learn

recorderbreathholescoversealgentlefirst notes

Say this to your child

“"The recorder is the school’s first instrument! Two golden rules: breathe GENTLE — a soft ‘too,’ never a hurricane — and cover the holes with flat finger pads, no leaks. Then the holes become your ladder: all fingers down is one note, lift one for the next, lift another for the third — and by Friday, you are playing songs."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a recorder — the first instrument of almost every school."
  2. The gentle rule: breathe a soft "too" into the mouthpiece — the recorder sings on GENTLE air. Blow hard and it squeaks like a startled mouse. Gentle first, always.
  3. The seal: cover a hole with a finger PAD — flat, full, no gaps. Test each hole: sealed = clear note; leaky = squeak. The recorder tells you the truth instantly.
  4. The hole ladder: all holes covered — note one. Lift one finger — note two. Lift another — note three. The holes ARE the ladder.
  5. Play the three-note game below and close: "gentle breath, sealed holes."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Recorder" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the recorder below — exactly as the school tube looks.

Ask your child

"Gentle breath or hurricane? What covers the holes — fingertips or flat pads? What happens when we lift one finger?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Soft ‘too,’ not a hurricane!" "All sealed — clear note!" or the ladder climber: "Lift one finger — new note!"

Out in the real world

Recorders live in every primary classroom on Earth — and their hole-ladder lives on flutes, clarinets and pan pipes: cover and release is how tubes make tunes. The two-dollar recorder is the honest door to all of them.

Try it together

Three-Note Songs: recorder ready, gentle breath. Learn the ladder: all-down, lift-one, lift-two — three clear notes. Then the first song: "Hot Cross Buns" is just the ladder walked — three-two-one, three-two-one, one-one-one-one, three-two-one! Play it slowly; play it proudly. Then compose: any three-note pattern, played twice — a brand-new song, world premiere tonight.

Understanding check

Ask: "What kind of breath? What covers the holes? What do we get when we lift a finger?" Gentle, flat pads, a new note — three answers and the first song is near.

Parent tips

The squeak is information, not failure: it means a leak or a hurricane — ask which, and the child self-corrects. And "Hot Cross Buns" is non-negotiable: it is the song every recorder player on Earth plays first, and joining that club feels enormous.

This lesson pairs with the Recorder flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Saxophone — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the saxophone’s wonderful identity crisis: it LOOKS like brass — golden, curvy, shiny — but it SINGS with a wooden reed like a clarinet. Shape is one family, voice is another.

What is this?

A saxophone is a golden metal tube, wide and curving, ending in an upturned bell: a single reed on the mouthpiece makes the buzz, the long metal body shapes it, and the sound comes out warm, husky and laughing.

What does it mean?

The sax is the perfect trick question: families of instruments are decided by HOW they make sound, not what they look like. Metal body, wooden voice — the sax teaches classification by listening, not looking.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sax ideas: golden and curvy like brass — but the voice comes from a single WOODEN reed, like the clarinet’s; the tube bends twice and flips its bell upward — built so the player can reach every key; and the voice is the laughing one — jazz’s favourite sound.

Why this matters

Look-versus-listen classification is a genuine thinking skill, and the sax is its most charming case. Plus the honk-to-smooth game is the best breath-and-reed warm-up two straws can provide.

What it teaches

Family classification by sound source, curved-tube length thinking, reed-breath control (honk versus smooth), and jazz listening — spotting the sax’s laugh in real music.

Words to learn

saxophonebrass shapereedwoodwindjazzhuskybell

Say this to your child

“"The saxophone is a trick! Golden, shiny, curvy — it dresses like the brass family. But its voice comes from a wooden reed, same as the clarinet — so it is really a WOODWIND in brass clothes! And its sound? Sometimes a cartoon duck, sometimes a slow, laughing song — jazz’s favourite voice, wearing gold."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a saxophone — the golden tube with a secret."
  2. The trick question: it looks like the brass family — shiny, golden, curvy. But listen: its voice comes from a single WOODEN reed, same as the clarinet. It is a woodwind wearing brass clothes!
  3. The curves: the tube bends twice — down, around, and the bell flips UP toward the listener. The bends let short arms reach a long tube.
  4. The voice: honk like a cartoon duck, then smooth like a slow song — both are the sax. The reed and the breath choose.
  5. Play the look-listen game below and close: "brass outside, woodwind inside."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Saxophone" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the golden sax below — its curves and upturned bell exactly as the instrument looks.

Ask your child

"Which family does the saxophone SOUND like? What makes its voice — lips or a wooden reed? Which music loves the saxophone most?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "A woodwind in brass clothes!" "The reed sings, not the lips!" or the jazz fan: "It sounds like laughing!"

Out in the real world

Saxes wail through jazz, soul and every big-city night — and their classification trick lives in every music book: sound source decides the family. Golden outside, wooden inside — meet any saxophonist and they will say exactly that.

Try it together

Look or Listen: three cards up — trumpet (brass), clarinet (woodwind), saxophone (both-looking). The rule: sort by SOUND. The leader hums or honks — bright lip-buzz (trumpet), woody flutter (clarinet), reedy-warm with a laugh (sax) — and players point to the family. Then the honk-to-smooth game: one straw-reed honk, then one long smooth hum — the sax’s two moods, both owned.

Understanding check

Ask: "What family is the sax by voice? What makes the sound? What are its two moods?" Woodwind, a wooden reed, honk and smooth — three answers and the jazz is in.

Parent tips

Say the rule out loud twice: families go by VOICE, not outfit. And the straw-reed from the clarinet lesson transfers — same reed, golden attitude.

This lesson pairs with the Saxophone flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Sitar — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the sitar — India’s long-necked wonder — and its shimmering secret: strings that buzz on purpose, and hidden strings that sing along by themselves.

What is this?

A sitar is a long-necked string instrument with a big gourd body: five main strings played over high curved bridges, plus a dozen sympathetic strings underneath that ring along by themselves. The curved bridges give every note its famous buzzing shimmer.

What does it mean?

The sitar’s buzz is engineering, not accident: the wide, curved bridge lets the string hum against it — a sparkle built into the design. And the sympathetic strings are music’s friendliest echo: strings that vibrate because OTHER strings nearby are singing.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sitar ideas: the neck is LONG — a whole ladder of notes stretching far; the bridge is curved, so every note shimmers with a buzz — on purpose; and sympathetic strings hide under the main ones and ring along like a ghost choir.

Why this matters

The sitar introduces resonance made visible — strings answering strings — and opens the world’s music beyond the orchestra: Indian classical music has its own grammar, and the sitar is its trumpet and its violin.

What it teaches

Resonance awareness (strings answering strings), drone-and-melody layering like the bagpipes’ lesson, cross-cultural listening, and gentle plucking over a long reach.

Words to learn

sitarneckgourdbuzzsympathetic stringsdroneshimmer

Say this to your child

“"The sitar is India’s wonder — a gourd, a VERY long neck, and strings that shimmer! The little bridges are curved, so every note buzzes sparkly. And here is the secret: under the main strings hide ghost strings — sympathetic strings — that ring along all by themselves when the big strings sing. One string plays; the ghost choir answers!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a sitar — India’s long-necked singing gourd."
  2. The long neck: trace it — so much longer than a guitar’s! Long neck means a huge ladder of notes to climb.
  3. The buzz: the little bridges are CURVED, and the string hums against the curve — that is the sitar’s famous shimmer, built in on purpose.
  4. The ghost choir: UNDER the main strings hide more strings — the sympathetic ones — that ring along whenever the main strings sing. Strings answering strings!
  5. Play the resonance game below and close: "one string sings, the others answer."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Sitar" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the sitar below — the long neck and gourd exactly as the instrument looks.

Ask your child

"Is the sitar’s neck long or short? Why does every note buzz? What do the hidden strings do?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The neck is a giant ladder!" "The buzz is on purpose!" or the ghost spotter: "The ghost strings sing along!"

Out in the real world

Sitars shimmer through Indian classical music and every Beatles-era film flashback — and resonance lives at home: sing loudly near a piano with the pedal down and hear its strings answer. Ghost choirs are everywhere.

Try it together

Ghost Strings: stretch two rubber bands over a box, side by side, NOT touching. Pluck one hard, hold it still — listen: the other band hums along, faintly. Sympathetic strings, live! Then the drone layer: one player hums a steady low drone; the other plucks a shimmering melody over it — the sitar’s two-layer music, at kitchen scale. Pluck, buzz, answer — India’s shimmer, understood.

Understanding check

Ask: "What shape are the sitar’s bridges? What do sympathetic strings do? What layers make the sitar’s music?" Curved, ring along, drone plus melody — three answers and the shimmer is heard.

Parent tips

The faint hum of the untouched band needs quiet rooms and close ears — lean in together. And the drone-plus-melody layer repeats the bagpipes’ lesson: one sound under, one sound dancing on top.

This lesson pairs with the Sitar flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Tambourine — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the tambourine’s double life: it is a DRUM (thump the skin) wearing a SHAKER (jingles around the rim) — and the famous trick is playing both voices at once.

What is this?

A tambourine is a shallow drum with metal jingles set in its rim: thump the skin with the heel of your hand for the drum voice, shake it for the jingle voice, or combine both — thump-and-shake — for the full tambourine.

What does it mean?

Two instruments share one hoop, and the combo pattern — thump-shake-thump-shake — is a genuine two-track coordination exercise: the hand thumps in rhythm while the wrist keeps the jingles rolling.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three tambourine ideas: the thump lands on the HEEL of the hand, near the edge — a drum voice; the shake lives in the WRIST — jingles rolling; and the combo is the star: thump-shake, thump-shake, both voices one pattern.

Why this matters

Two-voices-one-body is the tambourine’s gift — the same splitting the drum kit and piano ask for later, introduced on a hoop a four-year-old can hold.

What it teaches

Hand-heel striking with wrist shaking simultaneously, two-track rhythm, dynamic control (thump loud, jingle soft or both loud), and the confidence of holding a whole percussion section.

Words to learn

tambourinejinglesthumpshakecomborimboth at once

Say this to your child

“"The tambourine is two instruments in one hoop! Thump the skin with the heel of your hand — TOM, the drum voice. Shake the wrist — sh-sh-sh, the jingle voice. And the famous trick is BOTH at once: thump-SHAKE, thump-SHAKE! One hoop, two voices, one very happy player."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a tambourine — a drum wearing a shaker."
  2. Voice one, the drum: thump the skin with the heel of your hand near the rim — TOM. Two thumps, proud.
  3. Voice two, the shaker: wrist rolling — sh-sh-sh, the jingles whisper.
  4. The combo: thump-SHAKE, thump-SHAKE — drum and jingles in one pattern. That is the tambourine’s whole trick.
  5. Play the combo game below and close: "thump and shake, both at once."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Tambourine" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the tambourine and its jingles below — exactly as the double instrument looks.

Ask your child

"What makes the drum voice? What makes the jingle voice? What is the famous combo?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "TOM with my hand, sh-sh with my wrist!" "Thump-SHAKE — both at once!" or the proud owner: "I’m a two-instrument player!"

Out in the real world

Tambourines shake through pop choruses, gospel music and every music classroom — and the combo trick lives in any hoop with loose bolts or a jar of buttons: thump one surface, rattle another.

Try it together

Combo Call: leader calls "THUMP!" (heel, TOM) or "SHAKE!" (wrist, jingles) — player follows, getting faster. Then the combo round: "BOTH!" — thump-SHAKE rolling for eight beats. Finish as a band: thump-shake steady under a sung song, the tambourine carrying both halves of the rhythm alone. One hoop, whole section.

Understanding check

Ask: "Heel or fingertips for the thump? Where does the shake live? Name the combo." The heel, the wrist, thump-shake — three answers and the hoop has two voices.

Parent tips

The heel-of-hand thump protects fingers and sounds best — model it slow. And if no tambourine exists, a plate of dry pasta shaken while thumping a cushion splits the two voices just the same.

This lesson pairs with the Tambourine flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Trombone — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the trombone’s marvel: while every other brass instrument pushes buttons, the trombone player’s arm IS the buttons — stretching the tube longer and lower with one slide.

What is this?

A trombone is a brass trumpet-length tube with a SLIDE instead of valves: push the slide out, the tube grows, the notes sink; pull it in, the tube shrinks, the notes climb. It can even glide between notes — the famous wawa slide.

What does it mean?

The trombone makes pitch a visible, movable thing: the note lives at a slide POSITION, and the arm learns the map. It is the only instrument that can slide siren-smooth between notes — and the slide-whistle proves it free.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three trombone ideas: slide out = tube longer = notes LOWER; slide in = notes higher — the arm is the keyboard; and the glissando — sliding WHILE buzzing — makes the wawa swoop no other brass instrument can.

Why this matters

Length-pitch gets a whole arm here — the clearest, most physical version of the law the flute and horn taught — and the slide’s siren is the funniest, most memorable sound on the shelf.

What it teaches

Length-pitch mapping by arm extension, position memory, buzz control across the slide, and the glissando — continuous pitch, a rare and delightful skill.

Words to learn

tromboneslidestretchlowerglissandowawapositions

Say this to your child

“"The trombone has no buttons — it has a SLIDE, and your arm plays it! Push the slide out: the tube gets longer and the notes sink lower. Pull it in: shorter, higher! And the trombone’s famous trick is the wawa — buzzing WHILE sliding, gliding between notes like a siren. Your arm is the whole keyboard!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a trombone — the brass with no buttons, just a slide!"
  2. The law: slide OUT — tube longer — notes sink lower. Slide IN — tube shorter — notes climb. The arm plays the notes.
  3. Slide-whistle demo: blow a slide whistle, pushing the plunger out — the note sinks exactly like the trombone’s slide. Same physics, pocket edition.
  4. The wawa: buzz a note and slide slowly — waaaa-waaa — gliding between notes like a siren. No other brass can!
  5. Play the stretch game below and close: "out is low, in is high."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Trombone" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the trombone below — its long slide exactly as the instrument looks.

Ask your child

"What happens when the slide pushes OUT? What plays the notes — fingers or the arm? What is the sliding trick called?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Out is low, in is high!" "My arm is the keyboard!" or the siren joy: "Waaa-waaa — I glided!"

Out in the real world

Trombones swank through jazz bands, orchestras and every cartoon wah-wah-wah — and their law lives in every slide whistle and telescoping drinking straw: stretch the tube, sink the note.

Try it together

Arm Keyboard: slide whistle (or a drawn slide poster with positions marked). The leader calls "position one!" — close. "Position four!" — arm out far. Each position gets a hummed pitch: the arm learns the map. Then the wawa finish: buzz-hum while sliding slowly out — one giant glissando, room applause. Out is low, in is high — the trombone’s law, in the arm forever.

Understanding check

Ask: "Slide out makes notes what? What plays the notes? What is the glide called?" Lower, the arm, the glissando — three answers and the siren sings.

Parent tips

Mark slide positions on the poster — trombonists really do learn numbered positions. And the slide whistle is the honest home trombone: no buzz required, all the physics.

This lesson pairs with the Trombone flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Trumpet — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the trumpet — the smallest, brightest brass — where three little valves do the tube-length work and the player’s lips provide the engine: buzz first, buttons second.

What is this?

A trumpet is a brass tube about a metre long, folded into a handy shape with three valves: press a valve and the air detours through extra tubing, the tube effectively lengthens, and the pitch changes. The sound starts as a lip buzz.

What does it mean?

The trumpet is the brass engine made visible: the LIPS buzz (the engine), the VALVES steer the tube length (the gears), and the BELL throws the sound forward (the exhaust). Every brass instrument is this same machine, bigger or smaller.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three trumpet ideas: the sound starts with a lip RASPBERRY — brrr — that is the engine, and no lips means no sound; the three valves are buttons that make the tube longer — longer is lower; and the voice is the BRIGHT one — the trumpet is the brass family’s loudest hello.

Why this matters

The raspberry-into-a-tube demo is the honest first brass lesson — and the bright-versus-mellow contrast with the French horn completes the family map: same machine, different sizes and moods.

What it teaches

Lip buzzing (the foundational brass skill), valve-as-detour thinking, bright-vs-mellow tone sorting, and fanfare rhythm — short, proud calls.

Words to learn

trumpetvalvesbuzzlipsbrightfanfarebell

Say this to your child

“"The trumpet starts with a raspberry! Buzz your lips — brrr — that is the engine of ALL brass. Then the three valves: press one, and the air takes a longer detour through extra tubing — longer is lower! The result is the brightest hello in the orchestra: TA-DA! Short, proud fanfares are the trumpet’s home."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a trumpet — the brass family’s loudest hello!"
  2. The engine first: lips together, blow a raspberry — brrr! THAT is how all brass sound starts. No buzz, no music.
  3. The valves: three buttons. Press one and the air takes a detour through extra tube — longer tube, lower note. Buttons that stretch the trumpet.
  4. The voice: the trumpet is the BRIGHT one — sharp, clear, forward — the horn’s mellow opposite.
  5. Play the fanfare game below and close: "buzz, buttons, bright."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Trumpet" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the trumpet below — its three valves and bell exactly as the instrument looks.

Ask your child

"What buzzes — the trumpet or your lips? What do the valves do to the tube? Whose voice is brighter, trumpet or French horn?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "My lips are the engine!" "Valves stretch the tube!" or the fanfare: "TA-DA!"

Out in the real world

Trumpets lead every fanfare, royal announcement and mariachi band — and the buzz-engine lives at home: a raspberry blown through a paper tube is a trumpet’s honest cousin. Buzz and steer — that is all brass.

Try it together

Buzz Fanfares: raspberry-buzz into a rolled-paper tube (the trumpet). Short proud calls: TA! TA-TA! TA-DA! — echoed by the family. Then the valve game: one finger pinches the tube’s end on command ("valve down!") — the hum drops lower, the detour felt. Finish with a royal entrance: the trumpeter plays the fanfare, the whole family processes round the sofa. Buzz, buttons, bright.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the engine? What do valves change? What is the trumpet’s voice like?" The lip buzz, the tube length, bright — three answers and the fanfare is on.

Parent tips

Raspberries are the lesson, not a joke — practise them proudly and long. And paper tubes keep the buzzing honest: the tube gives the buzz a body, exactly like a real bell.

This lesson pairs with the Trumpet flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Tuba — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the tuba — the brass family’s giant: metres of tube coiled into a bear-hug shape, huffing the deep floor notes that every other instrument stands on.

What is this?

A tuba is the largest brass instrument: a huge coil of wide tubing ending in a great bell, played sitting down with the whole body wrapped around it. Its notes are the lowest in the band — the musical floor.

What does it mean?

The tuba completes the length law: the longest tube, the lowest notes. And its role is the foundation — oom-pah’s oom, the bass that makes every melody above feel grounded. Deep notes are carrying notes: you feel the tuba before you find it.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three tuba ideas: it is the BIGGEST and LOWEST of the brass — the family’s giant; the tube is metres long, coiled so a person can carry it; and its notes are the FLOOR of the music — everything else dances on top.

Why this matters

The tuba rounds out the brass size-spectrum — trumpet small-bright to tuba huge-deep — completing the family map, and its floor-note job is the child’s first lesson in musical foundations.

What it teaches

Size-pitch completion across the brass family, low-note humming, the oom-pah floor pattern, and the carrying-power of deep sounds.

Words to learn

tubagiantcoillowflooroom-pahdeep

Say this to your child

“"The tuba is the brass family’s giant! Metres and metres of tube — coiled round and round so you can carry it — and the deepest notes in the whole band. The tuba is the music’s FLOOR: hum low, oom… oom — and every song above stands on it. Oom-pah, oom-pah: that is the giant dancing under everything!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the tuba — the giant of the brass family."
  2. The giant’s tube: the biggest instrument needs the longest tube — metres of it! — coiled round and round so a player can carry it. Biggest coil, lowest notes.
  3. The floor: hum your lowest note — that is tuba country. Every melody above stands ON the tuba’s floor.
  4. Oom-pah: hum OOM (low), clap PAH (higher) — the tuba’s famous dance pattern from every brass band.
  5. Play the floor game below and close: "big coil, deep floor."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Tuba" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the big tuba below — exactly as the giant coil looks.

Ask your child

"Which brass instrument is biggest and lowest? Why is the tube coiled? What is the tuba’s job — the ceiling or the floor?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The giant of the brass!" "Metres of tube, coiled up!" or the floor-keeper: "Oom-pah — I hold the floor!"

Out in the real world

Tubas oom-pah through brass bands, polkas and New Orleans streets — and the floor-note idea lives under every song: listen for the low voice holding still while the melody dances. Find the floor in any tune today.

Try it together

Find-the-Floor: hum a simple melody while one player holds a steady LOW hum underneath — the song suddenly feels grounded, like furniture arrived. Swap roles. Then oom-pah band: half the family hums the low oom-oom, half claps the pah-pah — a whole brass-band floor, built of people. Big coil, deep floor.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who is the brass giant? Why coil the tube? What does the tuba build under the music?" The tuba, so it is carryable, the floor — three answers and the oom-pah is on.

Parent tips

Low humming is a full-body feeling — hands on the chest make it visible. And honour the floor role: children who love holding the bottom note are bass players in the making.

This lesson pairs with the Tuba flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Ukulele — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the ukulele — the guitar’s small, sunny cousin: four soft nylon strings, a body that fits small arms, and the friendliest first chord in all of music.

What is this?

A ukulele is a small four-string guitar from Hawaii: nylon strings that are kind to small fingers, a short neck that fits small hands, and a bright, sunny strum. Its name means "jumping flea" — the fingers dance that fast.

What does it mean?

The ukulele is the guitar’s lesson at half the difficulty: strum-pick lives here too, but the strings are soft, the stretches are small, and ONE finger can hold a whole chord. First real songs arrive in days, not months.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ukulele ideas: four strings, soft NYLON — gentle on fingertips, unlike steel; one finger can press a whole chord — the famous one-finger wonder; and the strum is a relaxed wrist brush — swish — the island heartbeat.

Why this matters

First-song-in-a-week is the ukulele’s superpower — and the confidence of actually PLAYING a song, tiny hands and all, is the musical milestone families remember.

What it teaches

One-finger chording (real harmony, immediately), wrist strumming, four-string tracking, and the joy of singing WHILE strumming — two-track, island style.

Words to learn

ukulelefour stringsnylonchordstrumHawaiiflea

Say this to your child

“"The ukulele is the guitar’s small, sunny cousin! Four soft nylon strings, a body that fits your arms — and the one-finger wonder: press one finger down and you hold a whole CHORD! Then the island strum: swish, swish, loose wrist — and suddenly you are playing a real song. Its name means jumping flea: your fingers dance that fast!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a ukulele — the guitar’s small, sunny cousin from Hawaii."
  2. The four strings: fewer than the guitar’s six, softer nylon, shorter neck — everything child-sized, on purpose.
  3. The one-finger wonder: lay ONE finger flat across a string pair — a chord! Harmony with one finger; the guitar asks for two or three.
  4. The island strum: loose wrist, brush down — swish. Brush up — swish. Swish-swish is the ukulele’s heartbeat.
  5. Play the first-song game below and close: "four strings, one finger, sunny swish."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Ukulele" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the small ukulele below — exactly as the sunny four-string looks.

Ask your child

"How many strings does a ukulele have? What are they made of — steel or soft nylon? How many fingers for the first chord?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Four strings, soft nylon!" "One finger — a whole chord!" or the strummer: "Swish-swish — I’m playing a song!"

Out in the real world

Ukuleles fill classrooms from Hawaii to Auckland to Vancouver — soft strings, small necks, fast songs. And the one-finger chord lives on every rubber-band box: one finger, one harmony, one very proud musician.

Try it together

First Song Tonight: box ukulele or real one. One-finger chord held, island strum going — swish, swish — while everyone sings a two-line song together (any favourite works). The strummer holds the chord the WHOLE song: one finger, real harmony, full song. Then the flea race: strum faster — swishy-swishy — the flea jumps! Sung, strummed, done: first concert, first encore.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many strings? Why are nylon strings friendly? What is the one-finger wonder?" Four, soft on fingers, the one-finger chord — three answers and the island sings.

Parent tips

Nylon before steel, always — finger-kind strings keep beginners strumming. And hold the chord FOR them the first song if needed: the strum plus the sing is the memory; the fingering follows.

This lesson pairs with the Ukulele flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Violin — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the violin — the smallest, highest member of the string family, balanced on the shoulder like it grew there, speaking in the voice closest to a human singing.

What is this?

A violin is the highest-voiced string instrument: held against the shoulder with the chin, fingers pressing the fingerboard strings, and a bow of horsehair drawn across them. Plucked it is pizzicato; bowed it sings and sings.

What does it mean?

The violin leads the orchestra for a reason: its range and its voice sit closest to the human singing voice — it can sob, laugh and soar. And its posture is a genuine skill: the instrument balances WITHOUT hands, leaving both free to play.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three violin ideas: it balances on the SHOULDER, held by the chin — no hands needed to hold it; the bow is the singing breath — slow and straight across the strings; and the size ladder: violin smallest and highest, viola bigger, cello bigger still, double bass the giant.

Why this matters

The shoulder-hold frees both hands for music — a postural marvel children find hilarious and then brilliant — and the string-family size ladder completes the map the cello started.

What it teaches

No-hands balance (posture as skill), slow straight bow strokes, the string-family size-pitch ladder completed, and expressive playing — the voice that can laugh.

Words to learn

violinshoulderchinbowstringspizzicatohighest

Say this to your child

“"The violin lives on your SHOULDER, held by your chin — no hands! — so both hands are free: one fingers the strings, one flies the bow. Draw the bow slow and straight, and the violin SINGS — the closest thing in the orchestra to a person’s voice: it can laugh, it can cry, it can soar. The smallest string, the highest song."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a violin — the singing string that lives on your shoulder."
  2. The balance: rest a cushion-box "violin" on the shoulder, chin holding it — hands OFF! It balances. That is the violin’s famous trick: both hands stay free to play.
  3. The bow breath: the bow is the violin’s breath — draw it SLOW and STRAIGHT across the strings and the instrument sings like a person.
  4. The family ladder: violin (small, highest) → viola → cello → double bass (giant, lowest). Same family, four sizes.
  5. Play the shoulder game below and close: "shoulder, chin, sing."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Violin" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the violin and its bow below — exactly as the singing string looks.

Ask your child

"Where does the violin rest — and what holds it there? What is the bow’s job? Which string family member is highest?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Shoulder and chin — no hands!" "The bow is its breath!" or the ladder-builder: "Violin, viola, cello, bass!"

Out in the real world

Violins lead every orchestra, soar over every film score and fiddle through every folk dance — and the no-hands balance lives in every toy-on-shoulder game. The singing bow needs only a rubber band and a slow finger.

Try it together

Shoulder Balance School: box violin on the shoulder, chin clamp, walk three steps without hands — giggling allowed, balance earned. Then the singing bow: rubber-band string, finger-bow drawn SLOW — a long singing note. Feelings round: "bow me a happy note… a sleepy one… a surprised one!" The same string sings them all — the bow decides. That is why the violin leads the orchestra.

Understanding check

Ask: "What holds the violin — hands or shoulder and chin? What does the bow draw? Name the family ladder." Shoulder and chin, the singing, violin-viola-cello-bass — three answers and the string sings.

Parent tips

Balance before bowing — the no-hands hold is the violin’s rite of passage and its funniest party trick. And slow bow strokes only: speed is noise; slowness is song.

This lesson pairs with the Violin flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Xylophone — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the xylophone — the wooden note ladder: bars from long-low to short-high, two mallets, and the cheeriest way to climb a scale with your own two hands.

What is this?

A xylophone is a row of wooden bars in pitch order — long bars low, short bars high — struck with mallets. Each bar speaks one bright, woody note, and the row is a ladder a child can walk by ear.

What does it mean?

The xylophone is the bells’ wooden cousin and the piano’s outdoor ancestor: the same ladder, but visible, touchable and impossibly cheerful. Two mallets make it a two-finger piano — patterns, jumps and runs within one small reach.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three xylophone ideas: long bar = low note, short bar = high note — the wooden ladder; two mallets, one in each hand — the friendly claw grip; and the bar’s centre rings true — strike the middle, not the edge.

Why this matters

The wooden ladder is the friendliest scale practice there is — bright enough to make errors delightful — and the two-mallet hold quietly rehearses two-hand keyboard playing.

What it teaches

Ladder walking by ear, two-mallet coordination, centre-striking accuracy, and pattern memory — runs, jumps and the famous downward slide.

Words to learn

xylophonebarsmalletsladdertapcentrewooden

Say this to your child

“"The xylophone is a ladder of wooden notes! Long bars on the left ring LOW, short bars on the right ring HIGH — and you climb it with two little mallets, one in each hand like holding two birds. Tap the MIDDLE of each bar for the true voice — tink! — and walk the ladder up, run it back down, then jump the rungs: the cheeriest scale in the world."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a xylophone — a ladder of wooden notes."
  2. The ladder: long bars left are LOW, short bars right are HIGH — the bells’ law, in wood.
  3. The claw: one mallet in each hand, held like holding little birds — loose, ready, two-handed from the start.
  4. The centre rule: strike the MIDDLE of the bar — the true voice lives there; edges go thumpy.
  5. Play the ladder games below and close: "long-low, short-high, tap the middle."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Xylophone" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration of the wooden bars and mallets below — exactly as the ladder looks.

Ask your child

"Which bars ring low — long or short? How many mallets? Where is the bar’s true voice?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Long is low, short is high!" "Two mallets — two birds!" or the ladder runner: "I ran the whole ladder down!"

Out in the real world

Xylophones plink through orchestras, school rooms and toy boxes — and the wooden ladder lives on every toy glockenspiel, water-jar row and fence-post line. Tap the middles; climb the rungs.

Try it together

Ladder Runs: xylophone (or jars, or taped paper bars). Walk the ladder UP — one bar, one tap, one hummed step. Run it back DOWN — the famous xylophone slide, woo-o-o! Then jumps: bottom bar to top bar, skips in between. Finish with the echo game: leader taps a three-bar pattern, player answers. Two mallets, one ladder, endless songs.

Understanding check

Ask: "Long or short for low? What do the two mallets hold like? Where do we strike?" Long-low, two birds, the middle — three answers and the ladder plinks.

Parent tips

Centre-striking is the sound rule — a week of "tap the tummy of the bar" beats months of edge-thumps. And alternate hands naturally: right-left-right-left up the ladder builds the two-hand habit for free.

This lesson pairs with the Xylophone flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Beat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the beat — music’s hidden heartbeat: the steady pulse that keeps marching under every song, whether anyone notices it or not.

What is this?

The beat is the steady pulse of music — the count you clap along to, the pulse your foot finds all by itself. Melodies wiggle above it, drums decorate it, but the beat just keeps walking: one, two, three, four.

What does it mean?

The beat is the difference between sounds and MUSIC: notes without a beat are a wind chime; notes WITH a beat are a song. Finding it — really feeling it — is the first and most permanent musical skill there is.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three beat ideas: the beat is STEADY — it does not speed up for excitement or stop for rests; your body finds it by itself — claps, stomps, head-bobs; and keeping it steady while others wiggle is a real job — the beat is music’s clock.

Why this matters

Steady beat underlies walking, reading rhythm, cutting with scissors and every instrument on the shelf. It is measurable, trainable, and four is exactly when the body wants to learn it.

What it teaches

Steady pulse keeping, tempo maintenance under distraction, body percussion, and the difference between beat (the clock) and rhythm (the pattern).

Words to learn

beatpulsesteadyclapstompclockheartbeat

Say this to your child

“"The beat is music’s heartbeat — the steady pulse underneath every song! Clap along with our song — feel it? Your hands found the pulse all by themselves. And the beat’s one law: STEADY. It does not rush, it does not stop, it just walks: one, two, three, four. Keep the clock, and the whole song has somewhere to live."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the beat — music’s heartbeat."
  2. Feel it: play any favourite song and clap ONLY on the pulse — not the words, the pulse underneath. "Your hands found it by themselves — that is the beat!"
  3. The steadiness law: the beat never rushes. March it slowly — one, two, three, four — the same speed, ten steps. Rushing is the one crime.
  4. Beat versus rhythm: the beat is the clock; the rhythm is the pattern danced ON the clock. Pat the beat while tapping a pattern — both live at once.
  5. Play the clock games below and close: "steady, steady, steady."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Beat" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly music illustration below — exactly as the pulse looks on the wall of the Music Room.

Ask your child

"What does the beat never do? What did your hands find in the song? What is the difference between the beat and the pattern on top?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The beat is the heartbeat!" "My hands found it by themselves!" or the steady one: "One, two, three, four — never rushing!"

Out in the real world

Beats tick everywhere: clocks, footsteps, windscreen wipers, skipping ropes. And every song on every radio carries one — find it together in the car: clap the pulse, hold it steady, arrive home in rhythm.

Try it together

Body Clock: pat knees on the beat to any song — steady, steady. Then split the body: feet STOMP the beat while hands clap a pattern on top — the clock and the dance at once. Finish with Beat Police: one player marches the beat; if the beat speeds up or stalls, the police call "STEADY!" and reset it. The clock is honoured; the song is safe.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the beat? What is its one law? What do our feet keep while our hands dance?" The heartbeat, steady, the clock — three answers and the song has a home.

Parent tips

Model slowness — children’s beats always rush; march like a sleepy giant. And praise the STEADY, never the fancy: a plain, unbroken beat is the trophy.

This lesson pairs with the Beat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Clap — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the clap — the first instrument every human owns: two hands, zero setup, and enough rhythm to carry whole songs.

What is this?

A clap is body percussion: hands striking each other in a rhythm. Claps keep the beat, copy patterns, answer drums and applaud the show — the most versatile sound a body makes.

What does it mean?

The clap is music’s portable laboratory: no instrument, no setup, any room, any time. Echo games on claps train listening memory, and the pattern games build the rhythmic sentences that all instruments later speak.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three clap ideas: claps can be LOUD (cupped hands, big air) or SOFT (flat fingers, whisper-clap) — two volumes in one pair of hands; the echo is the game — hear it, say it back exactly; and patterns are sentences — clap-clap-rest means something, and so does clap… clap-clap-clap!

Why this matters

Echo-clapping is the best aural-memory exercise ever invented for small musicians — and it needs nothing but the hands they came with.

What it teaches

Aural memory (echo patterns), dynamic control (loud-soft claps), rhythm sentence building, and turn-taking — the clapper listens before answering.

Words to learn

clapbody percussionechopatternloudsoftrhythm

Say this to your child

“"The clap is your first instrument — born right into your hands! Loud clap — cup your hands, big air. Whisper clap — flat fingers, soft. And the oldest music game on Earth: I clap a pattern, you clap it back EXACTLY — clap-clap-rest! Your ears are the teacher, your hands are the speaker."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is clap — the instrument you were born carrying."
  2. Two volumes: cupped hands — CLAP! Flat fingers — clap, the whisper. Do both; the hands have a dial.
  3. The echo: I clap two — you clap two. I clap clap-rest — you clap clap-rest. Exactly the same: the ears are the teacher.
  4. Build a sentence: clap-clap-REST… clap-clap-REST — the rest is part of the sentence! Then the long one: clap… clap-clap-clap — an echo in a pattern.
  5. Play the echo games below and close: "hear it, clap it back."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Clap" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly clapping illustration below — exactly as the body instrument looks.

Ask your child

"How do we make the loud clap? The whisper clap? What do our ears do in the echo game?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Cupped hands — CLAP!" "I echoed it exactly!" or the leader’s joy: "Now MY pattern for YOU!"

Out in the real world

Claps answer every song on every radio, cheer every show, and play pat-a-cake in every kitchen — body percussion is humanity’s oldest music and its most portable.

Try it together

Echo Circle: sit in a circle, one clap pattern travels player to player — each echoes it exactly, then adds ONE clap of their own. The pattern grows as it goes: clap-clap-rest → clap-clap-rest-clap → … by the time it returns, the sentence is enormous and the giggles are bigger. Loud claps, soft claps, rests — the whole rhythm section, born carried.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do the hands whisper? What does the echo start with? What is the hardest clap of all?" Flat fingers, the leader’s pattern, the rest — three answers and the circle echoes.

Parent tips

Keep patterns short at first — two to four claps: memory grows by success. And honour the REST: a held silence inside a pattern is the hardest and best clap of all.

This lesson pairs with the Clap flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Dance — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches dance — what happens when the beat climbs out of your clapping hands and moves into your whole body: music you do not just hear but BECOME.

What is this?

Dance is moving to music: steps, sways, spins and jumps that follow the beat and tell the song with your body. Every culture on Earth dances — it is music’s oldest way of being understood.

What does it mean?

Dance completes the musical body: ears found the beat, hands clapped it, and now the feet, hips and shoulders join. Full-body listening is the goal — and the freeze dance is its best trainer, because stopping ON the beat proves the body was truly listening.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three dance ideas: the body follows the BEAT — steps land on the pulse, not between; the music suggests the mood — sleepy songs sway, jumpy songs jump; and freezing is part of dancing — stop when the music stops, statue-still.

Why this matters

Full-body rhythm is the deepest musicality a four-year-old can own — and it is invisible in tests but obvious on every dance floor for the rest of their life.

What it teaches

Whole-body beat keeping, mood-to-movement mapping, start-stop control (the freeze), and expressive movement — the body telling the song.

Words to learn

dancemovefollowbeatfreezeswayspin

Say this to your child

“"Dance is the beat climbing into your whole body! March on the pulse — feet on the clock. Sway when the music is sleepy, jump when it is jumpy — the music suggests, your body answers. And when the music STOPS: freeze like a statue! Freezing is dancing’s proof — it shows your whole body was listening."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is dance — the beat living in your whole body."
  2. Follow the beat: play a song and march ONLY on the pulse — feet on the clock. Then let the hips sway, the shoulders bounce: the whole body joins the clock.
  3. Mood mapping: change the songs — a slow sleepy song: sway like seaweed. A jumpy song: hop like popcorn. The music suggests; the body answers.
  4. The freeze: when the music STOPS — statue! No wiggles, no giggles (well, a few). The freeze proves the feet were listening.
  5. Play the freeze dance below and close: "the body listens too."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Dance" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly dancing illustration below — exactly as the moving beat looks.

Ask your child

"What do our feet follow? What does sleepy music make the body do? What proves the body was listening?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Feet on the clock!" "Sleepy song — seaweed sway!" or the frozen statue: "FREEZE — nobody wiggles!"

Out in the real world

Dances live everywhere: weddings, kitchens, school gyms, the living-room carpet at 5pm. Put on any song tonight and march the pulse together — the beat is already in the room; dance lets it in.

Try it together

Freeze Dance: favourite songs on, everyone dances — full body, big joy. The pause button is the freeze caller: music off, STATUE, three seconds, music on, dance again. Five freezes, five statues, one enormous giggle. Then the mood round: sleepy song → seaweed; jumpy song → popcorn; royal song → slow proud marching. The body learned the whole language of music today.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the body follow? What does the freeze prove? Who suggests the mood?" The beat, the listening, the music — three answers and the whole body plays.

Parent tips

Statues get praised louder than dances — the freeze is the skill. And let the child press the pause button once: being the freeze-caller is as educational as freezing.

This lesson pairs with the Dance flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Harmony — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches harmony — what happens when a second note joins the tune and, instead of arguing, they agree: the warm, full sound underneath every great song.

What is this?

Harmony is notes sounding together on purpose: the melody sings on top, and one or more friendlier notes hum underneath, making the sound warm, full and rich. Solo = one voice; harmony = voices agreeing.

What does it mean?

Harmony is the musical version of teamwork: two different sounds choosing to fit. The ear hears the tune, but the chest feels the warmth underneath — and a child who can HEAR the underneath has learned to listen in layers.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three harmony ideas: harmony is at least TWO notes at once — the tune and its warm friend; the friend sits UNDER the tune and holds steady; and the test is the ear: agree, and it sounds rich; argue, and it sounds grumpy.

Why this matters

Layer-listening — melody above, harmony below — starts here and never stops: choirs, bands, film scores all live in layers. The family hum is the friendliest first harmony ever written.

What it teaches

Two-layer listening, pitch matching underneath a melody, steady holding while another moves (the harmony job), and agree-versus-grump discrimination.

Words to learn

harmonytogethermelodyunderneathwarmlayersagree

Say this to your child

“"Harmony is two notes agreeing! Sing a tune alone — lovely. Now a friend hums ONE steady note underneath — hear how the sound gets WARM and full? That is harmony: the tune dancing on top, the warm friend holding it up. And when the two notes argue — grumpy! — slide until they agree: rich!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is harmony — two notes agreeing to sound together."
  2. One voice, two voices: hum a tune alone. Now hum it WHILE a partner hums one steady low note underneath — hear the warmth bloom? That is harmony.
  3. The agree test: try a partner note that FIGHTS the tune — grumpy! Slide it until it fits — rich! The ear always knows.
  4. The harmony job: the tune moves; the harmony holds. Holding steady while another voice moves is a real musical skill — the anchor.
  5. Play the family harmony game below and close: "one tune, one warm friend."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Harmony" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly music illustration below — exactly as the agreeing notes look.

Ask your child

"How many notes make harmony? Where does the harmony friend sit — on top or underneath? What does the ear feel when they agree?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Two notes, agreeing!" "The warm friend underneath!" or the anchor: "I hold steady while the tune dances!"

Out in the real world

Harmony hums under every chorus, every hymn, every lullaby sung by two people — and the fastest test is the family hum: one voice sings the tune, the rest hum one low note. The living room blooms.

Try it together

Family Harmony: one singer sings any simple tune (a favourite works); everyone else hums ONE steady low note underneath — the anchor. Listen for the moment the warmth blooms — agree! Then try the grumpy note ON PURPOSE: slide the anchor wrong, hear it fight, slide it home. Agree-versus-grump, felt in the chest. Two layers, one song, a family in harmony.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is harmony? What is the harmony note’s job? What happens when notes argue?" Notes together, hold steady underneath, it sounds grumpy — three answers and the warmth blooms.

Parent tips

Low and steady wins the harmony — anchors hum LOW. And the grumpy-note experiment is essential: hearing the FIGHT teaches the FIT better than any explanation.

This lesson pairs with the Harmony flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Listen — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the quiet half of music: listening. Before any instrument speaks, somebody’s ears must be open — and listening is a skill you can practise like a game.

What is this?

Listening is receiving sound with attention: eyes closed, body still, ears wide. In music it means hearing what is actually there — high and low, loud and soft, near and far — instead of letting sounds wash past.

What does it mean?

Every lesson on this shelf depends on this one: the echo needs a listener, the harmony needs an ear, the beat needs a catcher. Listening is the invisible instrument — and it grows with practise, exactly like the drums do.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three listening ideas: stillness helps — ears work best when the body is quiet; sounds have knobs — high/low, loud/soft, near/far — and the hunter names them; and waiting is part of hearing — some sounds only arrive for patient ears.

Why this matters

Active listening is the root of attention itself — and the sound hunt turns it into a game children beg to play again, which is the entire trick of teaching attention at four.

What it teaches

Attention stamina, sound-discrimination (high-low, loud-soft), auditory figure-ground (finding one sound inside many), and the patience of waiting for quiet sounds.

Words to learn

listenearsstillhuntloudsoftpatient

Say this to your child

“"Listening is music’s quiet half — the half nobody plays and everybody needs! Sit still, close your eyes, and HUNT: what do you hear? High sounds, low sounds, loud ones, shy ones — every sound has knobs, and big ears name them. And some sounds are shy — they only arrive for patient waiters. Still body, wide ears: go."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is listen — music’s quiet half."
  2. The stillness: ears work best in quiet bodies. Sit still, close your eyes, and simply listen for ten seconds — the room is louder than you thought.
  3. The knobs: name what you hear — high or low? loud or soft? near or far? Every sound has knobs; hunters name them.
  4. The patient ear: some sounds are shy — the clock tick, the fridge hum. They arrive only for waiters. Wait for one.
  5. Play the sound hunt below and close: "still body, wide ears."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Listen" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly listening illustration below — exactly as the wide ears look.

Ask your child

"When do ears work best — wiggling or still? What knobs does every sound have? What kind of sounds arrive only for waiters?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Still body, wide ears!" "The fridge hums — low and shy!" or the hunter: "I heard THREE sounds with my eyes closed!"

Out in the real world

Big ears are free: the garden at dusk, the car window, the hallway’s quiet minute before bed. The sound hunt works anywhere — and children who hunt sounds at four hear music in layers forever.

Try it together

Sound Hunt: eyes closed, one minute, count the sounds you hear — then open up and list them together: clock, bird, fridge, footsteps, breath. Name each one’s knobs: high/low, loud/soft. Then the hiding game: one player makes a single sound — a tap, a hum, a shuffle — and the hunters say WHAT and WHERE. Big ears, big patience, big fun.

Understanding check

Ask: "What helps ears work best? Name a sound’s knobs. What do shy sounds need?" Stillness, high-low and loud-soft, patience — three answers and the ears are wide.

Parent tips

Model the stillness yourself — a listening grown-up is the best advertisement. And keep hunts short and triumphant: three sounds found beats ten sounds missed.

This lesson pairs with the Listen flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Lyrics — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches lyrics — the words inside the song: the story that rides on the melody, told in verses, choruses and sometimes just one repeated happy line.

What is this?

Lyrics are a song’s words: what the singer actually says. They tell the story, ask the questions, repeat the chorus — and the melody carries them the way a wave carries a boat.

What does it mean?

Words and music are two languages agreeing: the lyrics give the song its MEANING, the melody gives it its MOOD — and when they match (a sad word on a low note!), a four-year-old can hear the handshake.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three lyric ideas: lyrics are the WORDS — the story part of the song; the chorus is the part that comes back — the song’s home address; and words have moods that match their notes — happy words ride high, sleepy words drift low.

Why this matters

Lyric listening builds language AND music at once — the child who notices that the sad part of the song sounds sad has connected two whole worlds.

What it teaches

Language through song, mood-word matching, chorus recognition (structure!), and singing memory — lyrics are the stickiest words a child will ever learn.

Words to learn

lyricswordsversechorusstorymoodsing

Say this to your child

“"Lyrics are the words of the song — the story riding on the melody! Listen: the chorus is the part that keeps COMING BACK, the song’s home address. And here is the magic: happy words ride high bouncy notes, sleepy words drift on low slow ones — the words and the notes shake hands. Sing the story, and the song means something."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "These are lyrics — the words of the song."
  2. The two languages: sing any favourite — the WORDS tell the story, the TUNE gives the mood. Both at once: that is a song.
  3. The chorus: sing it twice — hear that part coming back? The chorus is the song’s home: it always knows the way back.
  4. Mood matching: sing a happy line HIGH and bouncy, then the same words LOW and slow — the words changed mood with the notes! Words and notes shake hands.
  5. Play the story games below and close: "words on the wave."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Lyrics" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration below — exactly as the song’s words look on the Music Room wall.

Ask your child

"What are lyrics? Which part keeps coming back? What happens to sleepy words on low slow notes?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The words of the song!" "The chorus is the home address!" or the mood-spotter: "Sad words go down low!"

Out in the real world

Lyrics live in every lullaby, every car-song, every chorus the family shouts on road trips — and the mood handshake is everywhere: listen to any cartoon song’s happy part. High, bouncy, agreeing.

Try it together

Sing-the-Story: pick a favourite family song. Sing the chorus twice — "there it is, the home address!" Then the mood game: sing one line happy-high, then sleepy-low, then whisper-mysterious — SAME words, three moods. The room votes on which mood matched best. Finish by making up ONE new line for the chorus — a family lyric, premiered tonight, remembered forever.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do lyrics give the song? What is the chorus? How do words and notes shake hands?" The story, the part that returns, mood matching — three answers and the song means something.

Parent tips

Chorus-hunting first: structure is the easiest listening win. And invented lyrics count double — writing one line makes every real lyric audible forever after.

This lesson pairs with the Lyrics flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Melody — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches melody — the tune itself: the single line of notes your ear follows through any song, the part you hum in the bath and cannot put down.

What is this?

A melody is a line of notes played one after another: the tune. It climbs, steps, jumps and rests — a path your ear walks. When you "can’t get a song out of your head," the melody is the part stuck there.

What does it mean?

Melody is music’s storyline in sound: ONE line at a time, going somewhere. Harmony and beat are the landscape; the melody is the path walking through it. Following that path with the ear — or drawing it with the hand — is music’s core skill.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three melody ideas: the melody is ONE line of notes in order — the tune; it moves like a path — up-steps, down-steps, big jumps; and the body can draw it: hand hills for the highs, valleys for the lows — the melody painted in the air.

Why this matters

Melody-following is the listening skill every other lesson here depends on — and hand-drawing the tune gives the ear a body, which is why music teachers have been air-painting melodies forever.

What it teaches

Melodic contour tracking (up-down-jump), hand-body mapping of pitch, hum-along memory, and the tune-versus-accompaniment distinction.

Words to learn

melodytunenotespathclimbjumphum

Say this to your child

“"The melody is the TUNE — the line of notes your ear follows through the whole song! It climbs like a hill, steps down like stairs, sometimes jumps like a frog. And your hand can draw it in the air: high notes up here, low notes down there. When a song sticks in your head, the melody is the part stuck — the tune is the traveller!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is melody — the tune itself."
  2. The path: hum any simple tune and trace it in the air — up here, down there, a jump! The melody is a path the hand can walk.
  3. The stuck-song test: what is the song part you hum in the bath? THAT is the melody — the line the ear cannot put down.
  4. Contour games: "sing me a melody that climbs… now one that tumbles down the stairs… now one with a JUMP!" The hand draws, the voice follows.
