  5. Play the follow games below and close: "one line, going somewhere."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Melody" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration below — exactly as the tune’s path looks.

Ask your child

"What is a melody — one line or many? How does it move? What does your hand draw when the tune climbs?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The tune! The part stuck in my head!" "Hills and stairs and frog-jumps!" or the air-painter: "My hand walks the melody!"

Out in the real world

Melodies live in every doorbell, ringtone and lullaby — and the air-drawing works on all of them: trace the ice-cream truck’s five notes in the air, hills and all. The ear learns the path; the hand remembers it.

Try it together

Air Painters: one player hums a simple tune while drawing it in the air — hills, stairs, jumps. Everyone else hums along and draws their own copy. Then reverse: the leader draws ONLY with the hand (no sound) — the players sing what the hand says! Contour becomes visible, singable, funny. Finish with the stuck-song share: everyone hums the tune stuck in THEIR head, hands painting. One line, going somewhere — every time.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the melody? How does it move through the air? What is stuck in your head after a song?" The tune, hills-stairs-jumps, the melody — three answers and the path is walked.

Parent tips

Draw BIG — contour needs whole arms, not fingertips. And simple tunes win: three to five notes make the clearest paths and the proudest painters.

This lesson pairs with the Melody flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Music — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the biggest word on the Music Room wall: MUSIC itself — what turns mere sound into songs, and how every card in this room is one piece of the one big picture.

What is this?

Music is sound organised by people on purpose: beats, notes, words and silence arranged so they mean something. A drop of rain is sound; twelve drops in a pattern are a rhythm — and rhythm with a tune is music.

What does it mean?

Every card on this wall is one organ of one body: the beat is the heart, the melody the voice, the harmony the warmth, the lyrics the story, listening the ears. The word MUSIC is the whole body — and this room is where its parts are learned.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three music ideas: music is sound ARRANGED — on purpose, with a plan; the plan has three big pieces — beat (the clock), melody (the path), harmony (the warmth); and silence is part of music — the rests belong to the song.

Why this matters

The big-picture lesson ties the whole room together: from here, every instrument card is a tool FOR music, not the point itself. Children who know what music IS can learn any instrument as a means, not a mystery.

What it teaches

Big-picture categorisation, connecting the room’s concepts (beat-melody-harmony-words-listen), and the idea that silence and planning make sound into art.

Words to learn

musicsoundorganisebeatmelodysilencetogether

Say this to your child

“"MUSIC is the big word: sound ARRANGED by people on purpose! Tap tap tap — random, just sound. Tap tap tap in a steady beat — music is arriving! Add a hummed tune, a warm harmony, words, even SILENCE — the rests belong to the song. Beat is the heart, melody is the path, harmony is the warmth: every card in this room is one piece of the one big word."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is MUSIC — the big word the whole room spells."
  2. Sound versus music: tap randomly — sound. Tap a steady beat — music is arriving. Add a hummed tune — music! Organisation is the difference.
  3. The three pieces: the BEAT is the heart, the MELODY is the path, the HARMONY is the warmth — every song ever sung has all three somewhere.
  4. The silence: clap… (hands wait)… clap — the wait was part of the rhythm! Silence belongs to music.
  5. Play the room-tour game below and close: "sound, arranged, felt."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Music" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration below — exactly as the big word looks at the centre of the Music Room wall.

Ask your child

"What turns sound into music? Name the three big pieces. Is silence part of music?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Sound arranged on purpose!" "Beat, melody, harmony!" or the quiet one: "The rests belong to the song!"

Out in the real world

Music is everywhere humans are — lullabies, anthems, jingles, humming in the kitchen — and every bit of it is the same recipe: sound, arranged on purpose, felt by everybody. Name the recipe in any song today.

Try it together

The Room Tour: walk the Music Room’s cards. At each one, the child names its piece of the big word: "Beat — the heart!" "Melody — the path!" "Harp — a tool FOR music!" Finish by building thirty seconds of music from scratch: a steady pat-beat, a hummed three-note melody, one harmony hum underneath, a rest before the final note. Sound, arranged, felt — the room’s whole word, performed by the family.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is music? What are its three big pieces? Does silence belong?" Sound arranged on purpose, beat-melody-harmony, yes — three answers and the big word is owned.

Parent tips

The random-vs-arranged tap demo is the whole lesson — do it twice. And end with the family performance: music MADE, not just named, is what the word means.

This lesson pairs with the Music flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Pitch — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches pitch — the highness or lowness of a sound: the ladder every note stands on, which your voice has been climbing since your first squeak and roar.

What is this?

Pitch is how high or low a sound is: a mouse squeaks HIGH, a giant stomps LOW, and every note lives somewhere on that ladder. Small, fast things make high pitches; big, slow things make low ones.

What does it mean?

Pitch is the most physical of musical ideas: size IS sound. Big drum, low boom; tiny bell, high ting. And the voice can climb the whole ladder — sliding from mouse to giant — which makes pitch the easiest musical knob to feel and the hardest to explain, unless you slide it.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three pitch ideas: pitch is HIGH or LOW — not loud or soft (that is volume!); big-slow things hum low, small-fast things squeak high; and the voice slides the whole ladder — siren slides teach pitch faster than any explanation.

Why this matters

Pitch separates music’s two most-confused ideas at once: high-low is NOT loud-soft — and the siren slide, plus the whisper-shout test, untangles both in one game.

What it teaches

Pitch discrimination (high-low), the size-pitch law, voice-slide control, and the pitch-versus-volume distinction — two knobs, finally separate.

Words to learn

pitchhighlowladdersqueakstompslide

Say this to your child

“"Pitch is the high-and-low of sound! The mouse squeaks HIGH, the giant stomps LOW — big slow things hum low, small fast things squeak high. And your voice can climb the whole ladder: siiiiren — slide up, slide down! But careful: high-low is NOT loud-soft — you can whisper HIGH and shout LOW. Two different knobs!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is pitch — how high or low a sound is."
  2. The size law: big slow giant — LOW stomp-hum. Small fast mouse — HIGH squeak-hum. Big is low, small is high: the whole ladder in two animals.
  3. The siren slide: hum from your lowest to your highest — siiiiren! Slide up, slide down, land on a high, land on a low. The voice just climbed the ladder.
  4. The mix-up test: whisper a HIGH squeak — quiet but high! Shout a LOW stomp — loud but low! Pitch and loudness are two different knobs.
  5. Play the ladder games below and close: "big is low, small is high."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Pitch" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly high-low illustration below — exactly as the ladder looks on the wall.

Ask your child

"Who hums lower — the giant or the mouse? What does the siren slide climb? Are high-low and loud-soft the same knob?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Big is low, small is high!" "Siiiiren — my voice slid the ladder!" or the knob-sorter: "Whisper-high, shout-low — different knobs!"

Out in the real world

Pitch runs the whole sound world: big dogs bark low, small dogs yip high; big cars rumble, mosquitoes whine. And every keyboard, bell row and guitar string is the ladder laid out to touch.

Try it together

Mouse-and-Giant: the leader calls an animal — MOUSE! ELEPHANT! BEE! BEAR! — and everyone moves AND hums at that animal’s pitch: tiny squeaks, floor-scraping lows. Then the siren ladder: slide up for "climbing the stairs," down for "sliding down the hill," freeze on a mystery pitch for "who am I — high or low?" Pitch, felt in the throat, named by the ear.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is pitch? What is the size law? Are high-low and loud-soft the same?" High or low, big-low and small-high, no — three answers and the ladder is climbed.

Parent tips

The whisper-high and shout-low test is the lesson’s crown — pitch and volume separate in one laugh. And pitch-by-animal beats pitch-by-number for small children every time.

This lesson pairs with the Pitch flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Song — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the song — where all the room’s pieces assemble: a beat to walk on, a melody to follow, words that mean something, and a feeling that makes it worth singing.

What is this?

A song is the full machine: a beat underneath, a melody on top, lyrics riding the melody, and a feeling holding it all together. Three-minute songs, lullabies, anthems — same recipe, endless dishes.

What does it mean?

The song is the reason this room exists: every instrument and every word on the wall is a part waiting to be assembled. Building one — even a silly two-line one — shows the child that songs are MADE, by people, and that they can make one.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three song ideas: a song is the pieces TOGETHER — beat + melody + words; songs have a shape — start, chorus (home), end; and the feeling picks the speed — lullabies crawl, celebration songs jump.

Why this matters

Song-building is the room’s graduation: the child who has assembled one song owns the recipe, and recipes get reused for life — every kitchen-sung birthday and road-trip chorus is this lesson, still running.

What it teaches

Assembly thinking (parts into whole), song structure (start-chorus-end), mood-to-tempo mapping, and the performing pride of a finished thing.

Words to learn

songtogetherassemblechorusfeelingstartend

Say this to your child

“"A song is the whole machine singing together! A beat underneath — pat pat. A melody on top — hum hum. Words riding the melody — and a feeling choosing the speed: lullabies crawl, party songs jump! Start, chorus home, end. And the best secret of all: songs are MADE by people — and today, so is ours."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a song — all the pieces, assembled and singing."
  2. The recipe: beat underneath (pat it), melody on top (hum it), words riding the melody (say it), feeling choosing the speed (feel it). Four parts, one song.
  3. The shape: songs have a start, a chorus that comes home, and an end — like a visit to grandma’s.
  4. The feeling knob: sing the same song as a lullaby (slow, soft) and as a celebration (fast, big) — the feeling changed the speed!
  5. Play the build-a-song game below and close: "pieces together, heart included."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Song" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration below — exactly as the finished thing looks on the wall.

Ask your child

"What four pieces make a song? What is the part that comes home? Who picks the speed?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Beat, melody, words, feeling!" "The chorus is the home!" or the composer: "OUR song — we made it!"

Out in the real world

Songs are the human constant: birthdays, lullabies, road trips, adverts — all the same recipe. Sing any family favourite tonight and name its parts out loud: beat here, chorus home, feeling loud.

Try it together

Build-a-Song in Ten Minutes: choose a topic (the dog, the rain, grandma’s soup). Beat: pat a steady pulse. Melody: hum three notes up and down. Words: one line about the topic ("The dog runs roun-n-nd!"). Chorus: repeat the line twice — it is now the home. Feeling: pick lullaby or party — the speed follows. Perform it twice, bow, name it, done: a family song exists forever. Pieces together, heart included.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the four pieces. What is the song’s home? What picks the speed?" Beat-melody-words-feeling, the chorus, the feeling — three answers and the machine sings.

Parent tips

Silly topics make brave writers — the dog’s tail beats "my feelings" every time. And the double performance is the point: the second sing-through is where the song stops being a project and becomes a SONG.

This lesson pairs with the Song flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Tempo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches tempo — the speed knob of music: the same beat walking slowly like an elephant or sprinting like a mouse, and the whole mood of a song changing with it.

What is this?

Tempo is how fast or slow the beat goes: the pulse’s speed dial. Lullabies crawl, marches walk, dance songs sprint — same notes, different tempo, entirely different feeling.

What does it mean?

Tempo proves the beat is a law with one adjustable part: the speed. Slow a song down and it sighs; speed it up and it giggles. The notes stay home — the feeling travels.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three tempo ideas: tempo is the beat’s SPEED — fast, slow and every step between; the same song changes mood with tempo — sleepy slow, giggly fast; and tempo needs a boss — the leader sets the speed and everyone follows it together.

Why this matters

Tempo control is the first ensemble skill — a group marching at one agreed speed is a small miracle of listening — and the tempo-dial game makes the boss-and-follow structure hilarious instead of hard.

What it teaches

Speed modulation on a steady beat, mood-tempo mapping, leading-and-following (the tempo boss), and stopping at speed changes without collapsing.

Words to learn

tempospeedfastslowdialleadermarch

Say this to your child

“"Tempo is the beat’s speed knob! Elephant tempo — sloooow pat pat. Mouse tempo — quick-quick-quick! And here is the magic: sing our song slow and it sighs, sing it fast and it giggles — same song, new mood. One player is the tempo boss: hands up, slow… hands down, sprint! Everyone follows one dial."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is tempo — the speed knob of the beat."
  2. The dial: pat the beat slowly — elephant tempo. Pat it fast — mouse tempo. Same beat, different dial.
  3. The mood change: sing any song slow — it sighs. Sing it fast — it giggles! The notes stayed home; the feeling travelled.
  4. The boss: one player is the tempo leader — hands high means slow, hands low-fast means sprint. Everyone follows ONE dial.
  5. Play the dial games below and close: "same beat, new speed."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Tempo" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly fast-slow illustration below — exactly as the speed knob looks.

Ask your child

"What does tempo change — the notes or the speed? What does a slow tempo make a song feel? Who sets the speed?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The speed knob!" "Slow song sighs, fast song giggles!" or the boss: "Hands up — elephant tempo, follow me!"

Out in the real world

Tempos rule every day: the walk-to-school tempo, the fire-drill sprint, the bedtime lullaby crawl — and every song on the radio carries one. Change the tempo of any family song tonight: the mood flips.

Try it together

Tempo Boss: one leader, everyone patting the beat. The leader’s hands are the dial: high and floating — elephant slow; low and dashing — mouse fast; frozen — STOP! Change tempos every eight beats — the band follows the dial through walk, crawl and sprint without dropping the beat. Then the mood test: our family song at three tempos — sleepy, walking, silly — and the room votes on the best one. Same beat, new speed, every time.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is tempo? What changes when the dial turns? Who does everyone follow?" The beat’s speed, the mood, the tempo boss — three answers and the band has a dial.

Parent tips

The freeze at tempo changes is the skill — model the STOP as part of the game. And let every child be the boss once: leading the dial is as musical as following it.

This lesson pairs with the Tempo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Tune — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the tune — the melody’s pet name: the specific line of notes that makes a song ITSELF, recognisable in as few as three notes.

What is this?

A tune is a song’s identifying melody: the exact line of notes that makes THIS song and no other. Hum three notes of a famous song and everyone knows it — the tune is the song’s fingerprint.

What does it mean?

Tunes are identity: hundreds of songs share the same twelve notes, but the ORDER makes each one itself. Recognising a tune in three notes is genuine ear skill — the child is matching sound-prints like a detective.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three tune ideas: the tune is a song’s own melody — its fingerprint; three notes can give it away — ears are brilliant detectives; and tunes can be hummed, whistled, tapped or played — the notes stay the same on any instrument.

Why this matters

Tune-matching is ear training wearing a game show costume — and it builds the recognition memory that language, faces and reading all quietly reuse.

What it teaches

Melodic recognition, short-sequence memory, transferring tunes across instruments (hum-to-tap-to-bell), and the delight of identification — ears as detectives.

Words to learn

tunefingerprintrecognisethree noteshumwhistlename

Say this to your child

“"A tune is a song’s fingerprint — its very own melody! Hum three notes of our favourite song… which one is it? See — your ears are DETECTIVES! And the tune survives any messenger: hum it, tap it on a pot, ring it on a bell, whistle it — different voices, same tune. The notes in a row are the identity!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a tune — the song’s own fingerprint."
  2. The fingerprint: hum three notes of a family-favourite song — "which song?" That is tune-recognition: three notes, whole identification.
  3. Same tune, new voice: hum the tune, then TAP it on a pot, then ring it on a bell — different sounds, SAME tune. The notes are the identity, not the instrument.
  4. The whistle test: whistled tunes still count — the tune survives any messenger.
  5. Play the detective games below and close: "three notes and I know it!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Tune" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration below — exactly as the fingerprint melody looks.

Ask your child

"How few notes can give a tune away? What stays the same when the tune moves from voice to pot to bell? What are our ears doing in the game?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Three notes — I know it!" "Same tune on the pot!" or the detective: "My ears solved it!"

Out in the real world

Tunes are the world’s ID cards: three notes of any cartoon theme and every child in the room spins round. And the messenger-swap works everywhere: tap the family song on the table tonight — recognition will roar.

Try it together

Name That Tune (family edition): one player hums THREE notes of a family-favourite song — the others guess. Too hard? Four notes. Too easy? Two! Then the messenger round: the same tune arrives hummed, then pot-tapped, then bell-rung — three deliveries, one fingerprint, endless delight. Ears as detectives, songs as suspects, the family as game show.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is a tune? How many notes can give it away? What stays the same across voice, pot and bell?" The song’s fingerprint, three, the tune itself — three answers and the detective ears are on.

Parent tips

Start with the family’s OWN songs — recognition needs familiarity first. And two-note rounds are the boss level: save them for the grand finale.

This lesson pairs with the Tune flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Volume — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches volume — music’s loud-soft knob: the dial that turns a whisper into a giant and back again, and the musician’s most social skill.

What is this?

Volume is how loud or soft a sound is: whispers, chatting, shouting — music uses the whole range. Soft for lullabies and secrets, loud for celebrations and fanfares, and the in-between for everything else.

What does it mean?

Volume is the musician’s manners AND their paint: a song that is loud all the way through is just noise; the QUIET parts make the loud parts land. Controlling the dial — growing, shrinking, stopping — is dynamics, and it starts with a game.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three volume ideas: volume is loud or SOFT — not high or low (that is pitch again!); the dial has many steps, not two — whisper, talk, big, GIANT; and growing and shrinking — getting louder and softer SLOWLY — is the real musician’s trick.

Why this matters

Dynamic control is the difference between playing an instrument and operating it — and the grow-quiet game builds it as pure joy, which is the only way it sticks.

What it teaches

Dynamic range control, crescendo-decrescendo (growing and shrinking), the pitch-versus-volume distinction reinforced, and the social sense of when loud is welcome.

Words to learn

volumeloudsoftwhispergiantdialgrow

Say this to your child

“"Volume is the loud-soft knob! Whisper it… talk it… BIG it… GIANT it — the dial has many steps. And the musician’s trick is the GROW: start soft as a secret and grow sloooowly to a giant — a sound sunrise! Then shrink back — a sunset. Soft parts make the loud parts land. That is how songs breathe."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is volume — the loud-soft knob."
  2. The dial: whisper it… talk it… BIG it… GIANT it — the same word at four volumes. The dial has steps, not just ends.
  3. The mix-up again: whisper HIGH, shout LOW — volume and pitch are still two separate knobs; one more game to prove it.
  4. The grow: start whisper-soft and GROW slowly to giant — a sound sunrise! Then shrink — a sunset. Growing and shrinking slowly is the musician’s trick.
  5. Play the dial games below and close: "soft to giant, slowly."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Volume" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly loud-soft illustration below — exactly as the dynamics dial looks.

Ask your child

"What is volume — high-low or loud-soft? Name the dial’s steps. What is the grow?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Loud or soft — the dial!" "Whisper, talk, BIG, GIANT!" or the sunriser: "I grew my sound from secret to giant!"

Out in the real world

Volumes fill every day: library-soft, playground-big, birthday-GIANT — and every song manages all of them. Listen for the quiet verse before the big chorus tonight: the dial at work.

Try it together

Sound Sunrise: everyone hums one note at whisper level. On the leader’s slow hand-raise, the hum GROWS — whisper, talk, big, GIANT — then sinks back down on the hand-lower: sunset. Three sunrises, three sunsets, zero shouting crashes. Then the opposite game: "loud librar-y?" — no! "Soft football stadium?" — no! The dial, its manners, and its drama, all owned.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is volume? What is the grow? Are loud-soft and high-low the same knob?" Loud or soft, growing slowly, no — three answers and the dial breathes.

Parent tips

The slow hand is the conductor’s trick — growing needs TIME to be musical. And celebrate the controlled GIANT: loud is welcome when it is shaped.

This lesson pairs with the Volume flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Band — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the band — a small crew of players where everyone owns a job and the groove belongs to everybody: the first lesson in playing WITH instead of alone.

What is this?

A band is a small group of musicians playing different jobs together: drums drive, bass holds the floor, guitars and keys fill the middle, a voice tells the story. Few players, big cooperation.

What does it mean?

The band is harmony’s next step: not just notes agreeing, but PEOPLE agreeing — each taking a job, staying in it, and trusting the others to stay in theirs. The groove only exists when everybody keeps their lane.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three band ideas: a band is a small crew — everyone has ONE job; the jobs stack — beat below, harmony middle, story on top; and the groove is shared — leave your lane and the whole sound wobbles.

Why this matters

Role-keeping inside a group is a deep social skill, and the band is its funniest, loudest classroom — children feel instantly why their job matters: the sound collapses without it.

What it teaches

Role assignment and keeping, ensemble listening (hearing yourself AND the others), turn-taking within songs, and the shared-groove idea — one sound, many hands.

Words to learn

bandcrewjobgroovetogetherlaneensemble

Say this to your child

“"A band is a small crew with one big sound! The drums keep the heartbeat, the bass holds the floor, the guitars fill the middle, and the voice tells the story. Everybody has ONE job — and the magic is that nobody leaves their lane: the groove belongs to everybody, so everybody keeps it. Play together, stay together!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a band — a small crew, one big sound."
  2. The jobs: drums = the heartbeat, bass = the floor, guitar/keys = the middle, voice = the story. Name a favourite song’s jobs by ear.
  3. The lane: each job stays in its lane — the drummer does not steal the singing; the lane IS the job.
  4. The shared groove: play a recording and point at each layer as it lands — hear how the lanes stack into one sound?
  5. Play the family-band game below and close: "own job, one sound."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Band" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly band illustration below — exactly as the crew looks on the wall.

Ask your child

"How many players make a band? What is the drummer’s job? What happens if someone leaves their lane?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Everybody has one job!" "Drums are the heartbeat!" or the bandmate: "I kept my lane — the groove held!"

Out in the real world

Bands play on every stage, street corner and school hall — and their lane-system is hearable in any song: point at the layers one by one. The family can BE a band tonight: pots, shakers, hums, one voice.

Try it together

Family Band: assign the jobs — one pot-drummer (heartbeat), one shaker (floor), one hummer (middle), one singer (story). Play a favourite song’s groove at kitchen scale: everyone starts their lane on the leader’s count. Then the challenge: one player swaps lanes mid-song — hear the wobble! — and swaps back — hear it heal! Own job, one sound: the band’s whole law, played by four people and a pot.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is a band? What does each player own? What is shared?" A small crew, one job, the groove — three answers and the band plays on.

Parent tips

Assign lanes BEFORE starting — bands rehearse their jobs, they do not invent them mid-song. And the mid-song wobble is the best teacher: let it wobble, name it, heal it.

This lesson pairs with the Band flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Chorus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the chorus — the sound of many voices singing one song together: nobody solo, everybody in, and the result bigger than any single voice.

What is this?

A chorus is a group singing together: a choir on stage, a family in the car, a classroom at assembly. Many voices, one song — voices of different sizes blending into one warm, big sound.

What does it mean?

The chorus is the anti-solo: the point is not WHO is singing but THAT everyone is. Blending means listening as much as singing — the chorus voice is half song, half ear.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three chorus ideas: a chorus is MANY voices on ONE song; blending beats starring — listen as much as you sing; and every voice changes the sound — the chorus is bigger BECAUSE nobody is missing.

Why this matters

Group singing is the most inclusive music-making there is — no instrument needed, any age, any size voice — and it teaches listening-while-doing, the deepest ensemble skill.

What it teaches

Group blending, singing-while-listening, shared tempo and pitch (holding the group’s key, not your own), and the belonging that comes from joining in.

Words to learn

choruschoirmany voicestogetherblendjoin inbig sound

Say this to your child

“"A chorus is many voices singing ONE song — a choir on stage, a family in the car, our whole room right now! The trick is blending: listen as much as you sing, until the voices melt into one big warm sound. And the best part: nobody is the star — the SONG is the star, and every single voice carries a piece of it."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a chorus — many voices, one song."
  2. The blend: hum the same note as a partner — listen more than you hum — until two voices sound like one warm voice. That is blending.
  3. The size of us: hum alone, then hum with three more voices — the sound DOUBLES in warmth without getting louder. That is the chorus trick.
  4. Nobody lost: in a chorus no voice is the star — the song is the star, and everyone carries it.
  5. Play the join-in games below and close: "many voices, one song."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Chorus" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly group-singing illustration below — exactly as the many voices look.

Ask your child

"How many voices sing in a chorus? What do we listen for while singing? Who is the star of a chorus?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Many voices, one song!" "Listen as much as you sing!" or the blender: "Our two voices melted into one!"

Out in the real world

Choruses sing in every church, school assembly, stadium and car — and the blend test works anywhere: hum with the radio, match the note, feel two voices become one. Joining in is the oldest music there is.

Try it together

The Join-In Round: one voice starts a familiar song alone. On the leader’s nod, one more voice joins — then another, then the whole room — each joiner matching the FIRST voice’s pitch, not their own. Listen to the sound grow warm with every voice. Then the reverse: voices drop out one by one until the first singer is alone again — hear how big WE were. Many voices, one song, nobody lost.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is a chorus? What beats starring? What happens to the sound with every voice that joins?" Many voices one song, blending, it grows warm — three answers and the room joins in.

Parent tips

Match-the-first-voice is the blend rule — the group follows the starter, not their memory. And praise listening louder than singing: a chorus of ears makes a chorus of voices.

This lesson pairs with the Chorus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Conductor — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the conductor — the musician who plays the BAND instead of an instrument: two hands, a small stick, and a hundred players watching every move.

What is this?

A conductor leads an orchestra without speaking: the raised hands set the tempo, the stick draws the beat in the air, and pointing brings players in or quiets them down. The conductor’s instrument is everybody else.

What does it mean?

The conductor is leadership made visible: no sound of their own, total responsibility for everyone else’s. Watching hands, staying together, starting and stopping as one — the skills are ensemble’s deepest, taught here in their purest form.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three conductor ideas: the conductor plays the BAND, not an instrument; big movements mean big sounds, small movements mean soft — the hands are the volume and speed dial; and the eyes never stop — conductors watch players, players watch hands: a circle of attention.

Why this matters

Leading-and-following without words is the quietest, most transferable game on the shelf — it rehearses attention, timing and the social magic of moving together.

What it teaches

Silent leadership, watching-hands attention, gesture-to-sound mapping (big-small, fast-slow), and the start-stop-together discipline.

Words to learn

conductorleadbatongesturefollowsilenttogether

Say this to your child

“"The conductor plays the whole BAND — with no instrument but two hands and a little stick! Big arms: the band plays big. Tiny waves: the band whispers. The stick draws the beat in the air — down-up, down-up — and a hundred players watch it like a clock. The conductor never says a word… and the whole orchestra listens."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the conductor — the musician who plays the whole band."
  2. The silent job: conductors never shout "faster!" — the HANDS say it. Big sweeping arms: big, bold sounds. Tiny fingertip waves: soft, gentle ones.
  3. The beat in the air: down-up, down-up — the stick draws the beat where everyone can see it. The air becomes the clock.
  4. The watching circle: players watch the hands, the conductor watches the players — nobody looks away. That circle IS the orchestra.
  5. Play the conductor games below and close: "watch the hands, play together."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Conductor" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly conducting illustration below — the raised hands exactly as the silent leader looks.

Ask your child

"What does a conductor play? How do the hands ask for soft? What do the players watch?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The conductor plays the BAND!" "Big arms — big sound!" or the leader: "My stick drew the beat in the air!"

Out in the real world

Conductors stand before every orchestra and choir on Earth — and the follow-the-hands game lives in every music classroom: one leader, silent hands, everyone watching. Lead your family song tonight with hands alone.

Try it together

Follow the Conductor: one conductor, everyone else humming (or tapping) a steady sound. The conductor’s hands are the dial: high sweep — grow big! Low fingers — shrink soft! Fast beating — speed up! Fist closes — STOP, frozen. Then swap conductors: every child leads once, and the room obeys their silent hands. No words the whole game — the circle of attention does the talking.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the conductor’s instrument? What do big arms ask for? What do players and conductor watch?" The band, big sounds, each other — three answers and the orchestra follows.

Parent tips

The conductor says NOTHING — the silence is the game’s engine; keep it even when the band wobbles. And big-vs-small gestures before fast-vs-slow: volume first, tempo second.

This lesson pairs with the Conductor flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Duet — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the duet — music built for exactly two: one part and another part, taking turns, answering each other, and joining forces for the final chord.

What is this?

A duet is a piece written for two players: piano duets at one keyboard, vocal duets sharing verses, instrument pairs trading melodies. Each part matters; neither is complete alone.

What does it mean?

The duet is the conversation lesson: I play, you answer; you lead, I follow. Between the solo (one voice) and the band (a crew) sits the duet — the smallest, most personal music team, where listening to ONE partner is the whole skill.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three duet ideas: a duet is exactly TWO players sharing ONE piece; the parts trade — one leads, one answers, then swap; and the ending is TOGETHER — duets finish on a shared chord, both hands (or voices) landing as one.

Why this matters

Turn-taking with sound is the duet’s gift — a musical version of conversation, with the same rule: listen first, then speak. It is the gentlest ensemble training there is.

What it teaches

Two-part turn-taking, musical question-and-answer, leading-and-following in pairs, and the shared final chord — landing together as the goal of every partnership.

Words to learn

duettwoparttradeanswertogetherfinal chord

Say this to your child

“"A duet is music for exactly TWO — one part for me, one part for you! I hum a question, you hum the answer. You lead, I follow, then we swap. And the ending is the best part: on the last note we both land TOGETHER — one shared chord, two players, one piece. That is a duet: the smallest team in music."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a duet — two players, one piece."
  2. The trade: I hum two notes — you hum two notes back. Question, answer! The duet’s oldest shape.
  3. The swap: now YOU lead the question and I answer. In a duet, both players do both jobs.
  4. The together-ending: play your part, I play mine — and on the last note, we BOTH land together: the shared chord. The duet’s whole point.
  5. Play the duet games below and close: "two parts, one landing."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Duet" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly two-player illustration below — exactly as the pair looks.

Ask your child

"How many players in a duet? What do the parts do — trade or play both at once? How does a duet end?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Two players, one piece!" "I asked, you answered — then we swapped!" or the lander: "Our final chord landed together!"

Out in the real world

Duets sit at every piano bench (four hands, one keyboard), harmonise in every pop chorus and trade solos in every jazz tune — and the question-answer game works with just two hums and two people.

Try it together

Question-and-Answer Duet: one player hums a two-note question; the partner answers with their own two notes — then they SWAP roles for four rounds. Then the shared-piece duet: player one holds a long hum (the floor), player two sings the tune on top — then swap. Finish with the landing: both parts glide to the SAME final note and hold it — one chord, two people, applause. Two parts, one landing.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many players? What is the oldest duet shape? Where do both parts land?" Two, question-and-answer, the final chord — three answers and the duet is played.

Parent tips

Keep the questions short — two to four notes: conversations need breathing room. And the shared final chord is non-negotiable: practise the landing until it is clean, then enjoy the pride.

This lesson pairs with the Duet flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Orchestra — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the orchestra — the biggest team music ever built: a hundred players arranged in families, strings in front, brass at the back, all breathing as one.

What is this?

An orchestra is a huge group of musicians: strings (violins, cellos) in front, woodwinds (flutes, clarinets) behind them, brass (trumpets, tuba) behind those, and percussion (drums, cymbals) at the back and sides — often a hundred players, one conductor, one sound.

What does it mean?

The orchestra is the room’s whole map in one place: every family on this shelf takes its seat, and the seating chart is the sound chart — quiet strings near the conductor, mighty brass at the back where their power needs room.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three orchestra ideas: the orchestra is the biggest music team — around a hundred players; the four families sit in order — strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion — quiet at the front, mighty at the back; and ONE conductor holds the hundred together — the team of teams.

Why this matters

The orchestra gathers every card on this wall into one picture — and its seating logic (soft near, loud far) is a spatial idea children grasp instantly and remember forever.

What it teaches

Family categorisation across the whole instrument wall, spatial-sound logic (seating = volume), big-team cooperation, and conductor-team structure.

Words to learn

orchestrafamiliesstringswoodwindsbrasspercussionhundred

Say this to your child

“"The orchestra is the biggest team in music — a HUNDRED players! Four families sit in order: the singing strings at the front, the breathing woodwinds behind them, the mighty brass at the back, the heartbeat percussion at the sides. And one conductor holds them all together with two hands and a stick. Every instrument we know lives here — all breathing as ONE sound."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is an orchestra — the biggest team in music."
  2. The four families: strings (the singing crowd), woodwinds (the breath players), brass (the mighty), percussion (the heartbeat). Name each family’s cards from our own wall.
  3. The seating logic: soft strings sit CLOSEST to the conductor, mighty brass at the BACK — loud instruments need room, quiet ones need to be heard.
  4. One conductor, hundred players: a hundred people, one pair of hands — and it works, because everyone watches.
  5. Play the family-orchestra game below and close: "four families, one sound."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Orchestra" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly orchestra illustration below — exactly as the big team looks.

Ask your child

"How many players in an orchestra? Name the four families. Which family sits at the back — and why?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "A hundred players!" "Strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion!" or the seating expert: "Brass at the back — they need room!"

Out in the real world

Orchestras fill every concert hall on Earth — and the seating chart is visible from any seat: find the strings’ fan around the conductor, the brass’s back row. Every children’s concert introduces the families — now yours already knows them.

Try it together

Family Orchestra: assign the room’s four families — hummers (strings, front), straw-reeds and bottles (woodwinds, middle), paper-tube raspberry brass (back), pot-and-shaker percussion (sides). The conductor raises the stick: one family plays at a time — strings… woodwinds… brass… drums! Then ALL families together for eight beats — the hundred-player sound at living-room scale. Bow, and the hall (sofa) goes wild.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many players? Name the four families in seating order. What holds a hundred players together?" A hundred, strings-woodwinds-brass-percussion, one conductor — three answers and the orchestra plays.

Parent tips

Play families SOLO first, then together — the layering IS the orchestral effect. And the paper-tube brass stays at the back even in the living room: the seating logic holds at every size.

This lesson pairs with the Orchestra flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Singer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the singer — the musician whose instrument is already inside them: breath for power, words for meaning, feeling for everything else.

What is this?

A singer is a musician who sings: they carry the melody AND the words AND the feeling — breath from the belly, words shaped clear, the story told face-first. Every culture’s first instrument was a voice.

What does it mean?

The singer completes the music-word chain: the lyrics lesson gave words their meaning, the melody gave them their path — the singer WALKS it, out loud, in front of people. Singing out is a courage skill as much as a music skill.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three singer ideas: the singer’s instrument is their own body — breath is the power, from the belly not the throat; words must be CLEAR — the story only lands if the words land; and singing OUT means singing to someone — the audience is part of the song.

Why this matters

The voice is the one instrument a child never leaves home without — and the confidence to sing OUT (not mumble-toward) transfers to every reading-aloud, show-and-tell and stage day of their life.

What it teaches

Breath support (belly breaths), clear diction through song, performing TO an audience, and the melody-plus-words integration the whole room has been building.

Words to learn

singervoicebreathbellywordssing outaudience

Say this to your child

“"The singer’s instrument is inside them — their own body! Breathe from the BELLY — hand on tummy, feel it move; that breath carries whole verses. Sing the words CLEARLY — the story only lands if the words land. And sing OUT — to someone, across the room! A shy mumble hides; a singer arrives. The voice: the instrument you never leave at home."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the singer — the musician whose instrument is inside them."
  2. The belly breath: hand on tummy, breathe so the hand moves — that is singing breath, deep and calm. Throat-breath runs out; belly-breath carries verses.
  3. The clear words: sing "the dog runs round" as mumble — nobody hears the story! Sing it CLEAR — every word lands. Singers tell stories; stories need words.
  4. Sing OUT: mumble-singing hides; out-singing ARRIVES. Pick someone across the room and sing TO them — the sound grows all by itself.
  5. Play the stage-singer game below and close: "breath, words, out."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Singer" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly singing illustration below — exactly as the story voice looks.

Ask your child

"Where does singing breath come from — throat or belly? Why must the words be clear? What does sing OUT mean?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Belly breath — feel my hand move!" "Clear words so the story lands!" or the performer: "I sang TO the whole sofa!"

Out in the real world

Singers lead every anthem, lullaby and birthday song on Earth — and the belly breath is the same one swimmers and storytellers use. Sing any favourite tonight TO someone: the arrival is the skill.

Try it together

The Stage Singer: sofa-arm stage, toilet-roll mic from the microphone lessons. Belly breath in, then sing a two-line story-song — any words, clear as bells — TO the audience, not at the floor. Audience job: applaud the clear words by name ("I heard DOG and ROUND!"). Three singers, three stories, one warm stage. Breath, words, out — the singer’s whole craft, at four.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does singing breath live? What must the words be? Where does the voice arrive?" The belly, clear, to the audience — three answers and the stage is yours.

Parent tips

Name-the-word applause trains diction better than "sing louder" ever will. And TO someone is the trick: giving the voice a destination makes it arrive.

This lesson pairs with the Singer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Solo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the solo — the spotlight moment: the band steps back, the room goes quiet, and one player carries the music all by themselves.

What is this?

A solo is one player performing alone: a guitar solo lifting out of a song, a singer’s unaccompanied verse, a cadenza where the orchestra stops and one violin soars. All eyes, one player.

What does it mean?

The solo is the room’s courage lesson: playing alone in front of people is a genuine bravery skill, and the solo’s structure makes it safe — the band returns, the spotlight is brief, the applause is certain.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three solo ideas: a solo is ONE player in the spotlight — the band steps back, not away; the solo is SHORT — eight shining beats can be a whole solo; and the audience is on your side — the quiet is attention, not judgement.

Why this matters

Standing alone and performing is one of childhood’s real mountains — the solo game climbs it in eight-beat steps, with the whole family as the kindest audience a soloist will ever have.

What it teaches

Solo performance courage, holding space alone (short but real), audience-relationship skills (bowing, thanking), and the return-to-the-band structure.

Words to learn

solospotlightalonebraveeight beatsbowapplause

Say this to your child

“"A solo is the spotlight moment — the band steps BACK, the room goes quiet, and one player carries it! And here are the secrets: a solo can be just EIGHT BEATS — short and shining is a real solo. The quiet audience is on your side — that silence is them leaning in. Play your eight beats, take your bow, and the band comes roaring back!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a solo — one player, one spotlight."
  2. The step-back: the band does not leave — it steps BACK and lowers to a hush, so the soloist floats on top. Hear it in any song: the sudden quiet around the solo.
  3. The short truth: a solo can be EIGHT BEATS — a little shine is a real solo. Long is not the point; brave is.
  4. The kind quiet: when the room goes quiet for a solo, that is ATTENTION, not judgement — the audience is leaning in.
  5. Play the spotlight game below and close: "one player, all ears."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Solo" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly spotlight illustration below — exactly as the one-player moment looks.

Ask your child

"How many players in a solo? What does the band do — leave or step back? What does the quiet audience mean?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "One player in the spotlight!" "Eight shining beats!" or the soloist: "The quiet was them leaning in — I played my solo!"

Out in the real world

Solos lift out of every song: the guitar break, the drum fill, the a-cappella verse — listen for the step-back tonight and name the solo when it arrives. Eight beats of shine, everywhere.

Try it together

The Spotlight: the family band plays a steady groove (pot, shaker, hum) — then the leader’s hand rises: the band steps to a hush, and the SOLOIST of the round plays eight shining beats alone — any instrument, any sounds. Hand falls: the band ROARS back. Every player gets a solo, every solo gets the full applause, every soloist bows. One player, all ears — courage, in eight-beat servings.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many players in a solo? How long must it be? What is the quiet audience doing?" One, eight beats is plenty, leaning in — three answers and the spotlight is yours.

Parent tips

Eight beats, exactly — the limit is what makes it brave instead of scary. And the band’s ROAR back is essential: the solo always ends in reunion, which is why children ask to solo again.

This lesson pairs with the Solo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).
